 15502  C. Automatic Extension of Visa Validity at POE for Contiguous Travel
 15503  
 15504      DHS changed the admission language in the provision relating to 
 15505  extension of visa validity in limited situations from ``shall'' to 
 15506  ``may'' to clarify that CBP always maintains the discretion to 
 15507  determine whether an alien is admissible and the appropriate period of 
 15508  admission. This change removes any ambiguity about whether CBP has an 
 15509  absolute duty to admit an alien to clarify that CBP has the discretion 
 15510  to admit an alien for a certain period of time, consistent with 
 15511  statutory and regulatory authorities. See new 8 CFR 214.1(b)(1).
 15512      DHS made technical revisions to the visa revalidation provisions 
 15513  allowing certain F, J, and M nonimmigrants to apply for admission if 
 15514  eligible for admission as an F, J, or M nonimmigrant if they are 
 15515  applying for admission after an absence from the United States not 
 15516  exceeding 30 days spent solely in contiguous territory or adjacent 
 15517  islands. See new 8 CFR 214.1(b). Such technical revisions include 
 15518  updating language to clarify that ``visa revalidation'' refers to 
 15519  automatic extension of visa validity at the POE to the date of 
 15520  application for readmission only. These provisions apply when, for 
 15521  example, a nonimmigrant finds himself or herself applying for re-entry 
 15522  after going to Mexico on spring break without realizing that his or her 
 15523  visa had expired. Instead of having to get a new visa, CBP may admit 
 15524  the nonimmigrant, whose visa validity is automatically extended by 
 15525  operation of DoS regulations. See 22 CFR 41.112(d). DHS does not 
 15526  believe it is necessary to require a nonimmigrant to obtain a new visa 
 15527  under these circumstances.
 15528      DHS made minor technical updates to account for inaccurate or no 
 15529  longer applicable terms and cites. First, DHS struck the reference to 
 15530  INA 101(a)(15)(Q)(ii) and reserved it, as that program no longer exists 
 15531  and is no longer in the INA.\301\ See new 8 CFR 214.1(b)(1)-(3). 
 15532  Second, DHS struck the reference to ``duration of status'' in 
 15533  redesignated 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(vii) and new 8 CFR 214.1(b)(1), 
 15534  214.2(f)(18)(iii), and 274a.12(b)(6)(v).
 15535  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 15536  
 15537      \301\ See Irish Peace Process Cultural and Training Program Act 
 15538  of 1998, Public Law 105-319, 112 Stat. 3013 (Oct. 30, 1998), as 
 15539  amended by Public Law 108-449, 114 Stat. 1526 (Dec. 10, 2004).
 15540  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 15541  
 15542  D. EOS
 15543  
 15544      This final rule will not create a new form for an EOS application. 
 15545  However, in the future, some form names and numbers may change. While 
 15546  DHS plans to update existing forms to allow F and I nonimmigrants to 
 15547  apply for an EOS
 15548  
 15549  [[Page 45100]]
 15550  
 15551  with USCIS, DHS believes it is more efficient to replace references to 
 15552  specific form names and numbers throughout the current regulations with 
 15553  generally applicable language.
 15554      Using general language in the regulatory text instead of referring 
 15555  to specific form names and numbers helps both DHS and stakeholders. It 
 15556  allows for technical changes without requiring an entirely new 
 15557  rulemaking to update form names. Stakeholders will receive notice and 
 15558  specific guidance on USCIS' website and in the appropriate form 
 15559  instructions, as they already do for various other benefits. Therefore, 
 15560  DHS uses this language in 8 CFR 214.1(c)(2) and struck the phrase 
 15561  exempting F and J nonimmigrants from filing an EOS, as they will be 
 15562  required to file an EOS if they wish to remain in the United States 
 15563  beyond their specified date of admission. See new 8 CFR 214.1(c)(2).
 15564      Additionally, DHS struck ``other than as provided in 214.2(f)(7)'' 
 15565  from new 8 CFR 214.1(c)(3)(v) and added in its place ``except those who 
 15566  fall under 8 CFR 214.1(m)'' to make it clear that students must apply 
 15567  for an EOS. This requirement will not apply to other nonimmigrants 
 15568  admitted for D/S, such as A-1 or A-2 representatives of foreign 
 15569  governments and their immediate family members; they will remain 
 15570  ineligible to file an EOS.
 15571      As part of the EOS application, USCIS requires biometric collection 
 15572  and may require such collection from F, J, and I nonimmigrants. USCIS 
 15573  has the general authority to require and collect biometrics from 
 15574  applicants, petitioners, sponsors, beneficiaries, or other individuals 
 15575  residing in the United States for any immigration and naturalization 
 15576  benefit. See 8 CFR 103.16. Biometric collection helps USCIS confirm an 
 15577  individual's identity and conduct background and security checks. 
 15578  Further, USCIS may also require any applicant, petitioner, sponsor, 
 15579  beneficiary or individual filing a benefit request, or any group or 
 15580  class of such persons submitting requests to appear for an interview. 
 15581  See 8 CFR 103.2(b)(9). USCIS may require such an interview as part of 
 15582  the screening and adjudication process that helps confirm an 
 15583  individual's identity, elicit information to assess the eligibility for 
 15584  an immigration benefit, and screen for any national security or fraud 
 15585  concerns.
 15586      The rule addresses the admission of F, J, and I nonimmigrants who 
 15587  timely filed an EOS and/or an application for employment authorization 
 15588  but left the United States before receiving a decision from USCIS. DHS 
 15589  anticipates this scenario will apply mostly to F-1 students applying 
 15590  for post-completion OPT and STEM OPT extensions.
 15591      While USCIS generally does not consider an application for EOS 
 15592  abandoned when the nonimmigrant leaves the United States,\302\ DHS 
 15593  recognizes the potential for conflict if a nonimmigrant receives 
 15594  authorization from both CBP and USCIS for what amounts to the same 
 15595  request (a specific period of time to pursue authorized activities). 
 15596  Where an alien in F, J, or I status timely files an application for 
 15597  EOS, leaves the United States before USCIS approves that EOS 
 15598  application, and applies for admission to continue his or her 
 15599  activities for the balance of the previously authorized admission 
 15600  period, USCIS would generally not consider the EOS application 
 15601  abandoned. See new 8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(i).
 15602  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 15603  
 15604      \302\ See U.S. Dep't of Justice, Memo from Cook, Acting Asst. 
 15605  Comm. Programs, Travel After Filing a Request for a Change of 
 15606  Nonimmigrant Status, HQ 70/6.2.9 (June 18, 2001), https://www.uscis.gov/sites/default/files/document/memos/Travpub.pdf.
 15607  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 15608  
 15609      Consistent with the general provision on admission in new 8 CFR 
 15610  214.1(a)(4) where the alien leaves the United States and applies for 
 15611  admission while his or her EOS application is pending and is admitted 
 15612  based on a new Form I-20 or DS-2019 after his or her previously 
 15613  authorized admission has expired; the pending EOS may be deemed 
 15614  abandoned. In this case, the AUD provided by CBP on the alien's I-94 
 15615  would govern. See new 8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(ii). This is because, in these 
 15616  cases, CBP's grant of a new period of authorized stay will supersede 
 15617  the pending EOS application seeking a period of authorized stay, 
 15618  rendering it superfluous.
 15619      DHS considered a policy whereby an F, J, or I nonimmigrant would 
 15620  automatically abandon an EOS application upon departing the United 
 15621  States. However, DHS believes such a strict requirement would not be 
 15622  practical, because people cannot always predict when they will have to 
 15623  travel. The decision to grant or deny an EOS, including in the event of 
 15624  a departure, involves an exercise of agency discretion, utilizing the 
 15625  laws, regulations, agency policy, and operational guidance.
 15626      Regarding applications for employment authorization for F-1 and J-2 
 15627  nonimmigrants, DHS notes that CBP does not adjudicate applications for 
 15628  employment authorization. Should an EOS application be deemed 
 15629  abandoned, USCIS will continue processing any applications for 
 15630  employment authorization, notwithstanding a departure, and, if the 
 15631  application is approved, USCIS will not issue an EAD with a validity 
 15632  date that exceeds the fixed date of admission provided to the alien at 
 15633  the POE. For example, an F-1 student wishing to engage in post-
 15634  completion OPT or a STEM OPT extension will need to file both an EOS 
 15635  application and an application for employment authorization. Where the 
 15636  alien had departed the United States before his or her applications are 
 15637  adjudicated, USCIS will not consider the employment authorization 
 15638  application abandoned. See new 8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(ii).
 15639      In all events, when an F-1 or a J-2 nonimmigrant travels while the 
 15640  employment authorization or EOS application is pending, he or she is 
 15641  still expected to respond to any RFE and to timely submit the requested 
 15642  documents. Because an RFE may arrive after an alien departs, either 
 15643  electronically or at a U.S. address, aliens traveling outside the 
 15644  United States while applications are pending are advised to make 
 15645  necessary arrangements to determine whether they have received an RFE 
 15646  relating to their application and to timely respond to any RFE.\303\ 
 15647  Failure to do so could result in USCIS denying an employment 
 15648  authorization or EOS application for abandonment.
 15649  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 15650  
 15651      \303\ See ICE, Traveling as an International Student, https://studyinthestates.dhs.gov/traveling-as-an-international-student (last 
 15652  visited Feb. 9, 2026). See also ICE, Travelling Outside the United 
 15653  States for Five Months or Fewer, https://www.ice.gov/sevis/travel 
 15654  (last updated July 8, 2025), which notes, ``Can I reenter if my 
 15655  request for OPT is pending? Yes, but traveling during this time 
 15656  should be undertaken with caution. USCIS may send you [an RFE] while 
 15657  you are away, however, so you will want to make sure you have 
 15658  provided a correct U.S. address both to your DSO and on the 
 15659  application and would be able to send in requested documents. Also, 
 15660  if USCIS approves your OPT application, you will be expected to have 
 15661  your EAD in hand to re-enter the United States. Like a request for 
 15662  further information, USCIS can only send the EAD to your U.S. 
 15663  address.''
 15664  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 15665  
 15666  E. Transition Period
 15667  
 15668  1. F and J Nonimmigrants Who Are in D/S on the Effective Date of the 
 15669  Final Rule
 15670      DHS will generally allow all F and J nonimmigrants present in the 
 15671  United States on the final rule's effective date who are validly 
 15672  maintaining that status and who were admitted for D/S to remain in the 
 15673  United States in F or J status, without filing an EOS request, up to 
 15674  the program end date reflected on their Form I-20 or DS-2019 that is 
 15675  valid on the final rule's effective date, for a period not to exceed 4 
 15676  years from the effective date of the final rule, plus an additional 60 
 15677  days for these F nonimmigrants and 30 days for J
 15678  
 15679  [[Page 45101]]
 15680  
 15681  nonimmigrants to depart the country. See new 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1).
 15682      F and J nonimmigrants who depart the United States after the rule's 
 15683  effective date and before the end date reflected on their Form I-20 or 
 15684  DS-2019 may be admitted with a new fixed admission period, like any 
 15685  other newly admitted F or J nonimmigrant, as provided for in new 8 CFR 
 15686  214.1(a)(4), based on the date on their Form I-20 or DS-2019 and 30 
 15687  days for departure. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5) or (j)(1)(ii). Aliens who 
 15688  need additional time to complete their current course of study, 
 15689  including requests for post-completion OPT, STEM OPT, or academic 
 15690  training, or would like to start a new course of study or exchange 
 15691  visitor program must apply for an EOS with USCIS for an admission 
 15692  period up to the new program end date, or OPT end date, listed on the 
 15693  Form I-20 or DS-2019, or successor form, reflecting such an extension, 
 15694  up to a maximum of 4-years. See new 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1).
 15695      For those aliens in F-1 status, admitted for D/S, present in the 
 15696  United States on September 15, 2026 who have timely filed on or before 
 15697  September 15, 2026 an application for post-completion OPT or a STEM OPT 
 15698  extension, there is not a requirement to file an EOS application, and, 
 15699  instead, they are only required to file the application for employment 
 15700  authorization for post-completion OPT or STEM OPT extension. See new 8 
 15701  CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i). An F-1 nonimmigrant who departs the United States 
 15702  before filing the application for post-completion OPT or STEM OPT, and 
 15703  is subsequently admitted to the United States with a fixed period of 
 15704  admission is required to file both an application for employment 
 15705  authorization, (Form I-765 or successor form) and an Application to 
 15706  Extend/Change Nonimmigrant Status (Form I-539, or successor form), 
 15707  pursuant to 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i)(B)(2) or (C). See new 8 CFR 
 15708  214.1(m)(1)(ii). An alien described in this section who departs the 
 15709  United States while the Application for Employment Authorization is 
 15710  pending or once approved will be admitted for a fixed period of time 
 15711  pursuant to 8 CFR 214.1(a). Id. DHS reserves the discretion to extend 
 15712  the period exempting the filing of the Application to Extend/Change 
 15713  Nonimmigrant Status (Form I-539 or successor form) in 6-month 
 15714  increments by publication of a notice in the Federal Register. See new 
 15715  8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(iii). The final rule moved this paragraph from 
 15716  paragraph (ii) to offer additional clarity, since such an extension can 
 15717  also apply to paragraph (i).
 15718      An F-1 nonimmigrant who departs the United States while the 
 15719  application for employment authorization for post-completion OPT or 
 15720  STEM OPT is pending or once approved will be admitted for a fixed 
 15721  admission period pursuant to new 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(iii). F-1 
 15722  nonimmigrants who file for employment authorization for STEM OPT remain 
 15723  eligible for the 180-day extension of their post-completion OPT EAD 
 15724  while their application for STEM OPT is pending pursuant to 8 CFR 
 15725  274a.12(b)(6)(iv).
 15726      Regarding pending applications for employment authorization during 
 15727  the transition period, aliens in F status who are subject to the 
 15728  transition and who are seeking post-completion OPT and STEM OPT 
 15729  employment authorization will be authorized to lawfully remain in the 
 15730  United States while the application is pending with USCIS if: (1) they 
 15731  are in the United States on the effective date of the final rule with 
 15732  admission for D/S; (2) they properly filed an application for 
 15733  employment authorization; (3) their application is pending on the final 
 15734  rule's effective date; and (4) they are not otherwise removable under 
 15735  the INA. Unless otherwise advised by USCIS, they will not have to file 
 15736  for an EOS or re-file an application for employment authorization. See 
 15737  new 8 CFR 214.1(m)(2). If the application for employment authorization 
 15738  is approved, the F-1 student will be authorized to remain in the United 
 15739  States in F-1 status until the expiration date of the EAD, plus 60 days 
 15740  as provided in their previous admission. If the employment application 
 15741  is denied, the F-1 student will continue to be authorized to remain in 
 15742  the United States until the program end date listed on their Form I-20, 
 15743  plus 60 days as provided in their previous admission, as long as he or 
 15744  she continues to pursue a full course of study and otherwise meets the 
 15745  requirements for F-1 status. See new 8 CFR 214.1(m)(2)(i).
 15746      Aliens in F-1 status with pending employment authorization 
 15747  applications, other than post-completion OPT and STEM OPT, also do not 
 15748  need to file for an extension or refile an employment authorization 
 15749  application. As long as these F-1 nonimmigrants continue to meet the 
 15750  requirements for F-1 status, they continue to be authorized to remain 
 15751  in the United States until the program end date listed on the Form I-
 15752  20, plus 60 days, regardless of whether the employment authorization is 
 15753  approved or denied. See new 8 CFR 214.1(m)(2)(ii).
 15754      As discussed in the NPRM, DHS believes that this transition will 
 15755  not be unreasonably burdensome on F and J nonimmigrants, and it will 
 15756  enable DHS to transition F and J nonimmigrants without unduly burdening 
 15757  nonimmigrants, USCIS, or CBP. Many would be able to complete their 
 15758  programs per the terms of their initial D/S using the original program 
 15759  end date as an expiration of their authorized period of stay. DHS may 
 15760  grant such periods, which include an additional 60 days for F 
 15761  nonimmigrants and 30 days for J nonimmigrants as provided in their 
 15762  previous admission, automatically without an application or fee. With 
 15763  this option, DHS believes that the majority of F and J nonimmigrants 
 15764  will be shifted to a fixed initial period of admission of 4 years or 
 15765  less. For example, J-1 research scholars and alien physicians who have 
 15766  program end dates for up to 5 or 7 years respectively will need to 
 15767  apply for an EOS before the 4-year maximum period of stay expires, 
 15768  i.e., the date that falls 4 years after the rule becomes effective and 
 15769  is listed in this rule for each program.
 15770      This will also allow DHS to transition F and J nonimmigrants to an 
 15771  admission for a fixed time period without unduly burdening them, USCIS, 
 15772  or CBP. It ensures that no F and J nonimmigrants remain in the United 
 15773  States indefinitely by requiring all F and J nonimmigrants admitted for 
 15774  D/S who wish to extend their stay beyond their program end date or the 
 15775  4-year maximum, whichever is applicable, to either file an EOS request 
 15776  or depart the United States and apply for admission at a POE by their 
 15777  program end date or the 4-year maximum period of stay from the 
 15778  effective date of this final rule, plus an additional 60 days for F 
 15779  nonimmigrants and 30 days for J nonimmigrants.
 15780      DHS considered the effect of transitioning to a fixed period of 
 15781  admission on F and J nonimmigrants originally admitted for D/S who 
 15782  chose to temporarily come to the United States to pursue a program of 
 15783  study or an exchange visitor program. DHS believes the changes will not 
 15784  significantly affect the interests of these nonimmigrants admitted in 
 15785  D/S. DHS is not changing the fundamental requirements to qualify for 
 15786  these nonimmigrant statuses, rather it is only changing the length of 
 15787  time that an individual may lawfully remain in the United States in F 
 15788  or J status without filing an EOS application. Admitting these 
 15789  classifications of nonimmigrants for a fixed period of admission simply 
 15790  confirms that the admission is temporary and clearly communicates when 
 15791  that temporary admission period ends. Further, as is the case for the 
 15792  fixed period of admission policy more generally, a fixed date of 
 15793  admission simply places these
 15794  
 15795  [[Page 45102]]
 15796  
 15797  nonimmigrants in the same position as most other nonimmigrants who are 
 15798  temporarily in the United States. They will still be able to continue 
 15799  to pursue their full course of study or exchange program; however, if 
 15800  they need additional time in F or J status, the burden will now be on 
 15801  them to request authorization directly from DHS and establish 
 15802  eligibility to extend their period of stay in such status, whereas 
 15803  previously they obtained an extension of lawful status in conjunction 
 15804  with a program extension through a DSO or RO.
 15805      At the same time, this process will provide immigration officials 
 15806  an opportunity to directly review and determine whether F and J 
 15807  nonimmigrants who wish to remain in the United States beyond their 
 15808  fixed period of admission are complying with U.S. immigration law and 
 15809  are indeed eligible to retain their nonimmigrant status. If there are F 
 15810  or J nonimmigrants relying on a D/S admission in an attempt to 
 15811  permanently remain in the United States, or otherwise circumvent their 
 15812  authorized status, this process will allow DHS to detect and deny an 
 15813  EOS request or entry under a new period of admission. DHS considered 
 15814  several alternatives in the NPRM before determining the above proposal 
 15815  was the best option.\304\
 15816  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 15817  
 15818      \304\ 90 FR at 42085-86 (Aug. 28, 2025).
 15819  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 15820  
 15821  2. I Nonimmigrants Who Are in D/S on the Effective Date of the Final 
 15822  Rule
 15823      I nonimmigrants who are in the United States on the effective date 
 15824  of the final rule will change from the existing D/S admission to a 
 15825  fixed date of admission. DHS is adopting the proposal in the NPRM for 
 15826  an automatic extension of the length of time it takes the alien to 
 15827  complete his or her activity, for a period of up to 240 days. See new 8 
 15828  CFR 214.1(m)(3). This is based on the period of stay authorized in 8 
 15829  CFR 274a.12(b)(20), which generally provides an automatic extension of 
 15830  employment authorization of 240 days to certain aliens whose status has 
 15831  expired but on whose behalf an application for an EOS was timely filed 
 15832  through a Form I-539, Application to Extend/Change Nonimmigrant Status, 
 15833  and which under new 8 CFR 214.2(i), has been generally applicable to an 
 15834  I nonimmigrant who changes information mediums.\305\ However, aliens 
 15835  who present a passport issued by the People's Republic of China (with 
 15836  the exception of a Hong Kong SAR passport or a Macau SAR passport), may 
 15837  be authorized an EOS until the activities or assignments consistent 
 15838  with the I classification are completed, but the EOS must not exceed 
 15839  the maximum period of 90 days. See new 8 CFR 214.1(m)(3). DHS believes 
 15840  that adopting an already established timeframe, to which I 
 15841  nonimmigrants are already accustomed, is reasonable. Consistent with 
 15842  the current process, an I nonimmigrant who departs the United States 
 15843  after the effective date of this final rule and would like to return to 
 15844  the United States in that same status will need to reapply for 
 15845  admission as an I nonimmigrant at a POE.
 15846  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 15847  
 15848      \305\ See USCIS, Instructions for Application to Extend/Change 
 15849  Nonimmigrant Status, https://www.uscis.gov/i-539 (last updated Jan. 
 15850  9, 2026).
 15851  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 15852  
 15853      I nonimmigrants on D/S who seek to remain in the United States 
 15854  longer than the automatic extension period provided are required to 
 15855  file an EOS request with USCIS. \306\ Id. In addition to I 
 15856  nonimmigrants being familiar with the timeframe under 8 CFR 
 15857  274a.12(b)(20), DHS anticipates that this provision will reduce any 
 15858  gaps in employment due to USCIS' processing timeframes between the I 
 15859  nonimmigrant's application for extension and USCIS approval of the 
 15860  application. It will also facilitate an I nonimmigrant's ability to 
 15861  complete his or her assignment while temporarily in the United States 
 15862  on behalf of a foreign media organization, it that it will give ample 
 15863  time to any I nonimmigrant to either complete that assignment or ask 
 15864  for an extension, as needed.

 15866  
 15867      \306\ In FY 2024, fewer than 38,000 aliens entered the U.S. in I 
 15868  classification. See DHS FY 2024, Quarter 4, tbl.4B, supra note 11.

content.text:
**Examining Relevant Sections**

I've zeroed in on the specifics, particularly lines 15371-15377 and 15695-15701 from the provided documents. I'm focusing on the implications for aliens departing the US without an approved EOS application, and then seeking readmission with a valid Form I-20. This seems central to the issues at hand.


**Analyzing Key Regulatory Text**

I'm now diving into the specifics of 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A), comparing it against the initial finding. It looks like the program end date on the I-20 or DS-2019 is the main factor determining stay, up to four years, plus 30 days. To be thorough, I'm also going to analyze Section V.F and Sections V.I-V.K. That should comprehensively cover DHS's perspective on F-1 classification!

[2026-14439: lines 15885-16264 of 19533, FR page 45102]
 15885  F. Requirements for Admission, Extension, and Maintenance of Status of 
 15886  F Nonimmigrants
 15887  
 15888      Under this final rule, as outlined in the proposed rule, DHS has 
 15889  changed the regulations that provide the framework for admission, 
 15890  extension, and maintenance of status for F nonimmigrants. These changes 
 15891  will eliminate D/S, require students to file an EOS if requesting to 
 15892  remain in the United States beyond the period of their admission, and 
 15893  clarify terms to ensure that the activities an F nonimmigrant has 
 15894  engaged in are consistent with those of a bona fide student.
 15895  1. Admission for a Fixed Time Period
 15896      In the NPRM, DHS proposed striking the previous regulation that 
 15897  allows F nonimmigrants to be admitted for D/S while also proposing to 
 15898  replace it with a provision allowing F nonimmigrants to be granted 
 15899  status for the length of their program, not to exceed 4 years. See 
 15900  proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i) and (f)(7)(vi). This is retained in the 
 15901  final rule with additional clarity added to new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i). 
 15902  More specifically, that paragraph references instances when additional 
 15903  time may be granted to an F-1 student by adding language to reference 
 15904  the completion of their program of study, as described in paragraphs 
 15905  (f)(7) and (f)(8)(iv) of that section and the beginning of a new 
 15906  program of study, as described in paragraphs (f)(5)(ii)(D) and (f)(7) 
 15907  of that section.
 15908      Second, the NPRM proposed retaining in the regulations the 
 15909  statutory limitation that restricts public high school students to an 
 15910  aggregate of 12 months of study at any public high school(s) while also 
 15911  clarifying that the 12-month aggregate period includes any school 
 15912  breaks and annual vacations. This is retained in the final rule with 
 15913  clarification that a public high school may also include a charter 
 15914  school or other similar school funded by U.S. taxpayers. See new 8 CFR 
 15915  214.2(f)(5)(i)(C). Current requirements, including paying the full cost 
 15916  of education, also remain in place.
 15917      Third, F-1 students who are applying to attend an approved private 
 15918  elementary or middle school or private academic high school will 
 15919  continue to be covered by the provisions of 8 CFR 214.2(f)(6)(i)(E). 
 15920  These provisions require the DSO to certify a minimum number of class 
 15921  hours per week prescribed by the school for normal progress toward 
 15922  graduation. See 8 CFR 214.2(f)(6)(i)(E). However, like all other F-1 
 15923  students, they will be subject to the 4-year maximum period of 
 15924  admission, and they will need to apply for an EOS with DHS if staying 
 15925  beyond this period. This is retained in the final rule. See new 8 CFR 
 15926  214.2(f)(7)(vi).
 15927      Fourth, DHS proposed exempting part-time border commuter students
 15928  
 15929  [[Page 45103]]
 15930  
 15931  from the general length of admission provisions. The regulations at 8 
 15932  CFR 214.2(f)(18) would continue to govern these border commuter 
 15933  students, including that DHS continue to admit them for a fixed time 
 15934  period. This is retained in the final rule. See new 8 CFR 
 15935  214.2(f)(5)(i)(B).
 15936      Fifth, F-1 students in a language training program will be 
 15937  restricted to an aggregate of 24 months of language study, which will 
 15938  include breaks and an annual vacation. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)(A). 
 15939  This limitation is a way to prevent abuse of the F-1 program. Public 
 15940  Law 111-306, enacted on December 14, 2010, and effective since 2011, 
 15941  requires language training schools enrolling F-1 students to be 
 15942  accredited by an accrediting agency recognized by the ED. DHS has found 
 15943  students enrolling in lengthy periods of language training, in some 
 15944  cases for more than two decades.\307\ DHS has also identified students 
 15945  who enrolled in language training programs despite previously being 
 15946  enrolled in or completing undergraduate and graduate programs requiring 
 15947  English language proficiency.\308\ Unlike degree programs that 
 15948  typically have prescribed course completion requirements, there are no 
 15949  nationally-recognized, standard completion requirements for language 
 15950  training programs and students are able to enroll in language training 
 15951  programs for lengthy periods of time. The lengthy enrollment in a 
 15952  language program, including enrollment in language courses for long 
 15953  periods subsequent to completion of a program of study that requires 
 15954  proficiency in English, raises concerns about whether the F-1 
 15955  nonimmigrants meet the statutory definition of a bona fide student with 
 15956  the intent of entering the United States for temporary study.\309\ 
 15957  Therefore, there is a 24-month aggregate limit for F-1 students to 
 15958  participate in a language training program, as it will provide a 
 15959  reasonable period of time for students to attain proficiency while 
 15960  mitigating DHS's concerns about the integrity of the program. This 
 15961  timeframe generally comports with the amount of time needed to gain the 
 15962  highest level of English proficiency under the Cambridge English 
 15963  Exam.\310\ This is retained in the final rule.
 15964  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 15965  
 15966      \307\ For example, one student has been enrolled in ELT programs 
 15967  at nine different schools since January 3, 2003. This student is 
 15968  active in SEVIS, reportedly studying English full time as of May 7, 
 15969  2025--accounting for more than 22 years of language training. The 
 15970  student's most recent school issued a program extension changing the 
 15971  student's program end date from January 2, 2025, to January 2, 2026. 
 15972  The school input the following reason for the extension: ``Student 
 15973  pursuing advanced level linguistic studies.'' The school's 2025 
 15974  catalog contains no references to linguistic studies--advanced or 
 15975  otherwise--and indicates the school offers general English academic 
 15976  preparation, TOEFL preparation, and business English courses. DHS 
 15977  analysis of data in SEVIS and valid as of May 7, 2025.
 15978      \308\ SEVIS Records show that for example a student who entered 
 15979  the country in 2005 studied English and then between January 2011 
 15980  and December 2024, he enrolled in a bachelor's program in Biology/
 15981  Biological Sciences, a master's program in Biotechnology, and a 
 15982  second master's program in Bioinformatics. He also engaged in post-
 15983  completion OPT and two periods of STEM OPT. Each of his Forms I-20 
 15984  indicated the academic programs required English proficiency, and 
 15985  the student had English proficiency. However, in January 2025, the 
 15986  student transferred to a language training school and remains active 
 15987  in SEVIS reportedly engaged in ELT as of May 7, 2025. DHS found at 
 15988  least 20 similar examples. DHS analysis of data in SEVIS and valid 
 15989  as of May 7, 2025.
 15990      \309\ See INA 101(a)(15)(F).
 15991      \310\ See Cambridge English, supra note 195.
 15992  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 15993  
 15994      Sixth, DHS proposed students with pending employment authorization 
 15995  applications who are admitted based on the DSO's recommended employment 
 15996  end date for post-completion OPT or STEM OPT specified on their Form I-
 15997  20, with a notice issued by USCIS indicating receipt of the Application 
 15998  for Employment Authorization, Form I-765 or successor form for post-
 15999  completion OPT or STEM OPT, and who cease employment authorized 
 16000  pursuant to a post-completion OPT- or STEM OPT-based EAD that expires 
 16001  before the alien's fixed date of admission as noted on their Arrival/
 16002  Departure Record (Form I-94 or successor form), be considered to be in 
 16003  the United States in a period of authorized stay from the date of the 
 16004  expiration noted on their EAD until the fixed date of admission as 
 16005  noted on their I-94 (unless the student violates the terms of the 
 16006  authorized stay). This is retained in the final rule. See new 8 CFR 
 16007  214.2(f)(5)(i)(D).
 16008      Seventh, the authorized period of stay for F-2 dependents cannot 
 16009  exceed the authorized period of stay of the principal F-1 student. DHS 
 16010  proposed adding this requirement and retains this proposal in the final 
 16011  rule. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)(E).
 16012  2. Changes in Educational Objectives
 16013      Prior to the implementation of this final rule, all F-1 students 
 16014  who change from one educational level to another or pursue multiple 
 16015  degrees in the same educational level are considered to be maintaining 
 16016  status. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii). DHS has observed that some 
 16017  students continuously enroll in different programs at the same degree 
 16018  level, such as by pursuing multiple associate, master's, undergraduate, 
 16019  bachelor's, or certificate programs. Alternatively, some students 
 16020  change to a lower educational level, such as completing a master's 
 16021  degree and then changing to an associate's program or an ELT 
 16022  program.\311\ This has enabled some aliens to remain in the United 
 16023  States for lengthy periods of time in F-1 student status, raising 
 16024  concerns about the temporary nature of their stay. In 2024, DHS 
 16025  identified nearly 77,000 F-1 students who have spent more than 10 years 
 16026  in student status since SEVIS was implemented in 2003.\312\ This 
 16027  includes individuals who enrolled in programs at the same educational 
 16028  level as many as 19 times, as well as students who completed graduate 
 16029  programs and then enrolled in undergraduate programs, including 
 16030  associate's degrees.\313\
 16031  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16032  
 16033      \311\ Id.
 16034      \312\ DHS analysis of data in SEVIS and valid as of Mar. 17, 
 16035  2025.
 16036      \313\ Id.
 16037  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16038  
 16039      DHS has also observed a pattern of students immediately 
 16040  transferring schools or changing educational levels or programs of 
 16041  study upon their arrival in the United States. These students often use 
 16042  an admission letter and Form I-20 from a well-known school to increase 
 16043  their odds of obtaining a student visa and then immediately request a 
 16044  transfer to their intended school or program of study once they have 
 16045  gained admission to the United States. Some of the most egregious 
 16046  examples are those who apply to a 4-year university, which requires 
 16047  demonstration of sufficient English level skills for enrollment in 
 16048  classes through the passage of the Test of English as a Foreign 
 16049  Language test (commonly known as TOEFL), receive their visa based on 
 16050  their declared intention of attending a 4-year university, and then 
 16051  transfer to English language programs upon arrival. Other, more 
 16052  dangerous examples, include those foreign students who receive a visa 
 16053  based on their declared intention to study the humanities, but then 
 16054  transfer into sensitive programs such as nuclear science. A handful of 
 16055  those have been arrested for spying for China.\314\ The existing 
 16056  regulations are vulnerable to exploitation by aliens who threaten U.S. 
 16057  national security. This rule is designed to reduce this vulnerability. 
 16058  Since 2020, there have been over 13,000 F-1 students who transferred 
 16059  before the start of classes or within their first term, including over 
 16060  4,400 students transferring from a higher education to ELT program of 
 16061  study within their first
 16062  
 16063  [[Page 45104]]
 16064  
 16065  term or session of a program of study.\315\ The number of F-1 students 
 16066  who changed their educational levels within the first 60 days of their 
 16067  program is close to 8,400.\316\ While the number of students 
 16068  transferring or changing educational levels represents a small 
 16069  percentage of the total F-1 student population, these transfers are 
 16070  often promoted by third-party recruiters and other for-profit entities 
 16071  to allow aliens to use the student visa process to mask their intent in 
 16072  the United States or circumvent F-1 restrictions.\317\ In addition, 
 16073  school officials are often burdened with the administrative costs of 
 16074  processing SEVIS transfer requests from F-1 students who misrepresented 
 16075  their intentions of studying at their institution.
 16076  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16077  
 16078      \314\ See CNN Politics, Chinese Engineer Sentenced to 8 years in 
 16079  US Prison for Spying, supra note 82, and Senate Select Committee on 
 16080  Intelligence Hearing (Feb. 13, 2018), supra note 82.
 16081      \315\ See SEVIS Data on Initial Transfers and Change of 
 16082  Education Counts (Mar. 31, 2025).
 16083      \316\ Id.
 16084      \317\ On May 29, 2020, President Trump signed a Presidential 
 16085  Proclamation to suspend the entry as nonimmigrants of certain 
 16086  students and researchers from the PRC. See Suspension of Entry as 
 16087  Nonimmigrants of Certain Students and Researchers from the People's 
 16088  Republic of China, Proc. No. 10043, 85 FR 34353 (Jun. 4, 2020). 
 16089  Since this proclamation, students often circumvent enforcement of 
 16090  this proclamation by applying to a permissible program of study to 
 16091  obtain a student visa and admission to the United States and then 
 16092  transferring or changing their program of study to engage in 
 16093  studies, research, and other activities that are prohibited. This is 
 16094  also a tactic used by international and third-party recruiters. See 
 16095  Inside Higher Ed., Gaming the Student Visa System (Jan. 12, 2024), 
 16096  https://www.insidehighered.com/news/global/international-students-us/2024/01/12/international-admission-offices-plagued-fraud-and.
 16097  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16098  
 16099      While there may be legitimate cases of students who wish to change 
 16100  their educational objective to gain knowledge at a lower or the same 
 16101  educational level, the traditional path of study typically progresses 
 16102  from a lower educational program to a higher one. The existing 
 16103  regulations present a model consistent with the majority of bona fide 
 16104  students who follow this traditional trajectory. The term ``full course 
 16105  of study'' as defined in the existing regulations requires that the 
 16106  program ``lead to the attainment of a specific educational or 
 16107  professional objective.'' \318\ Repeated changes to a program of study 
 16108  either within the same educational level or to move to a lower level, 
 16109  as well as immediate changes to a program of study upon initial entry 
 16110  into the United States, are not consistent with attainment of such an 
 16111  educational or professional objective. This understanding was reflected 
 16112  in the preamble to a 1986 rulemaking proposing changes to the F 
 16113  regulations, which stated: ``The proposed regulation. . .places 
 16114  limitations on the length of time a student may remain in any one level 
 16115  of study. Thus, the Service has eliminated applications for [EOS] for 
 16116  students who are progressing from one educational level to another but 
 16117  has placed a control over students who, for an inordinate length of 
 16118  time, remain in one level of study.'' \319\ But, by 1991, INS 
 16119  eliminated all EOS applications and began to rely on DSO's to make the 
 16120  decision on whether educational progress was being made. In the decades 
 16121  that have followed, it has become clear that this has enabled thousands 
 16122  to stay here for decades by switching programs and not making any 
 16123  upward progress.\320\
 16124  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16125  
 16126      \318\ 8 CFR 214.2(f)(6)(i).
 16127      \319\ Nonimmigrant Classes; Change of Nonimmigrant 
 16128  Classification, 51 FR 27867 (Aug. 4, 1986).
 16129      \320\ By reviewing SEVIS data as of Apr. 6, 2025, DHS has 
 16130  identified 2,137 aliens who first entered as F-1 students between 
 16131  2000 and 2010 and remain in active F-1 status today.
 16132  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16133  
 16134      Consistent with the NPRM, DHS is restricting school transfers and 
 16135  changes of educational objectives within a student's first academic 
 16136  year of a program of study, unless an exception is authorized by SEVP, 
 16137  and prohibiting F-1 students in a graduate level program of study from 
 16138  changing educational objectives at any point during their program of 
 16139  study. F-1 students in a graduate level program of study are also 
 16140  prohibited from transferring, but the proposed regulatory text has been 
 16141  amended to allow SEVP to authorize an exception to this prohibition due 
 16142  to extenuating circumstances. ``Educational objectives'' refers to an 
 16143  F-1 student's educational level or major. See new 8 CFR 
 16144  214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A) and new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i). DHS believes these 
 16145  changes will accommodate the legitimate academic activities of bona 
 16146  fide students, such as a desire to pursue a different field of study or 
 16147  more specialized studies in their current field. These changes will 
 16148  also provide SEVP with flexibility to grant exceptions for extenuating 
 16149  circumstances. For example, an exception may be appropriate when a 
 16150  school closes or when a school has a prolonged inability to hold in-
 16151  person classes due to a natural disaster or other causes. DHS has also 
 16152  clarified in the final rule that extenuating circumstances include 
 16153  students needing to change schools to complete elementary or secondary 
 16154  education.
 16155      In addition, an alien who has completed a program as an F-1 
 16156  nonimmigrant at one educational level will be unable to maintain F-1 
 16157  status, depart and be admitted in F-1 status, or otherwise obtain F-1 
 16158  status (e.g., via a change of status) through a program at the same 
 16159  educational level or a lower educational level. See new 8 CFR 
 16160  214.2(f)(5)(ii)(C). However, an F-1 student who has completed a program 
 16161  in the United States at one educational level and is beginning a new 
 16162  program at a higher educational level will be considered to be 
 16163  maintaining F-1 status if they otherwise comply with requirements under 
 16164  8 CFR 214.2(f). See new 8 CFR 214.2 (f)(5)(ii)(B). These provisions 
 16165  were retained from the NPRM to the final rule. They will be applied 
 16166  prospectively. Any programs completed prior to the effective date of 
 16167  the rule will not be counted towards the limits.\321\
 16168  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16169  
 16170      \321\ For example, an F-1 student who completed a master's 
 16171  degree prior to the effective date of the rule would be eligible to 
 16172  enroll in and be admitted for the completion of another master's 
 16173  degree. Any programs completed after the effective date of the rule 
 16174  would be counted towards the new limits of this rule.
 16175  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16176  
 16177      DHS believes that it is reasonable for a student to progress to a 
 16178  higher educational level rather than continue at the same level or 
 16179  pursue a lower level of education, as that is the traditional 
 16180  trajectory in the pursuit of higher education. Movement within the same 
 16181  level after completion of a program to a lower educational level raises 
 16182  concerns regarding whether the F-1 student is a bona fide student who 
 16183  intends to temporarily and solely pursue a full course of study rather 
 16184  than pursuing different degrees as a de facto way to prolong their stay 
 16185  in the United States.
 16186      If an F-1 student who has completed their first academic year of a 
 16187  program of study seeks to change educational objectives and this change 
 16188  would require an EOS, the alien would then apply for EOS using the form 
 16189  designated by USCIS, paying the required fee and following all form 
 16190  instructions, including submitting any biometrics required by 8 CFR 
 16191  103.16. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(D).
 16192      DHS recognized that these changes might require updates to SEVIS 
 16193  and other systems. Because the timeframe for those updates is not fixed 
 16194  and there could be technical issues regarding implementation, DHS is 
 16195  including a provision whereby DHS may delay or suspend implementation, 
 16196  in its discretion, if it determines that the change in educational 
 16197  level limitation is inoperable for any reason. The need for this 
 16198  provision is not indefinite and therefore DHS has added language in the 
 16199  regulatory text to clarify that this provision can be used for up to 
 16200  two years from the effective date of the rule (i.e., September 14, 
 16201  2028). See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(E). If DHS delays or suspends the 
 16202  provisions in this section governing the change in educational 
 16203  objectives, DHS will make an
 16204  
 16205  [[Page 45105]]
 16206  
 16207  announcement of the delay or suspension by notice in the Federal 
 16208  Register and to the academic community through SEVP's various 
 16209  communication channels, including ICE.gov/sevis, Study in the States 
 16210  (https://studyinthestates.dhs.gov), and SEVIS Broadcast Message. DHS 
 16211  will also announce the implementation dates of the change in degree 
 16212  level provision through SEVP's communication channels (ICE.gov/sevis, 
 16213  Study in the States, and SEVIS Broadcast Message) at least 30 calendar 
 16214  days in advance.
 16215      Additionally, DHS is retaining the term ``educational'' with 
 16216  respect to a change in level as DHS believes it accurately reflects 
 16217  current academic models. Specifically, ``educational'' captures 
 16218  programs for non-degree students, whereas using a term such as 
 16219  ``degree'' may not. For example, an F-1 student currently will not 
 16220  qualify for additional post-completion OPT if he or she changes to a 
 16221  non-degree certificate program, given that the certificate program is 
 16222  not a ``higher educational level.'' Similarly, certificate programs for 
 16223  professional advancement are typically not considered to be a ``higher 
 16224  educational level'' allowing students to qualify for additional post-
 16225  completion OPT.
 16226      DHS believes these changes will encourage F-1 students to complete 
 16227  the programs of study for which they were admitted to the United States 
 16228  and to only pursue additional programs of study that demonstrate an 
 16229  upward progression in degree levels, which is expected from a qualified 
 16230  bona fide student who is coming to the United States temporarily and 
 16231  solely to pursue a course of study. DHS believes that this restriction 
 16232  will not significantly impact the choice of bona fide students who come 
 16233  to the United States temporarily to complete a full course of study. 
 16234  The F-1 program, with its statutory requirement that an alien be a bona 
 16235  fide student who seeks to enter the United States temporarily and 
 16236  solely for the purpose of pursuing a full course of study at the school 
 16237  listed on his or her Form I-20 or successor form, should not be used by 
 16238  aliens wishing to remain in the United States indefinitely. These 
 16239  changes will better ensure that this statutory intent is fulfilled 
 16240  without hindering the options presented to bona fide students seeking 
 16241  study at higher educational levels and thus create a balanced solution 
 16242  to this issue.
 16243  3. Preparation for Departure
 16244      DHS retains its proposal from the NPRM to change the departure 
 16245  period for F nonimmigrants from 60 to 30 days. See new 8 CFR 
 16246  214.2(f)(5)(v). DHS received comments on this change, and those 
 16247  comments are discussed elsewhere in this preamble. DHS made this change 
 16248  for several reasons as discussed in the NPRM. The 60 days previously 
 16249  provided to F-1s to prepare for departure was twice as long as that of 
 16250  other SEVP programs (M and J nonimmigrants). See new 8 CFR 
 16251  214.2(j)(1)(ii) and 8 CFR 214.2(m)(10)(i). In addition, this 60-day 
 16252  period is also six times longer than certain nonimmigrants who are 
 16253  authorized to remain in the United States for years but are only 
 16254  provided with a 10-day period to depart the United States.
 16255      As discussed within the NPRM, DHS believes that 30 days for the F 
 16256  nonimmigrant population is the appropriate balance between a 60-day and 
 16257  a 10-day period of departure and has retained the proposed 30-day 
 16258  departure period for F-1 nonimmigrants in the final rule.\322\ 
 16259  Similarly, DHS notes that seeking an EOS or change of status is an 
 16260  allowable activity for F-1 nonimmigrants during the 30-day departure 
 16261  period following the completion of their program and incorporated this 
 16262  clarification in the proposed rule and retains it in the final rule. 
 16263  See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v).
 16264  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

[2026-14439: lines 16265-16644 of 19533, FR page 45105]
 16265  
 16266      \322\ 90 FR at 42089 (Aug. 28, 2025).
 16267  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16268  
 16269      DHS has also retained its proposal to clarify that an F-1 student 
 16270  who has completed a course of study and any authorized practical 
 16271  training will be allowed an additional 30day departure period which is 
 16272  reflected in the AUD on the Form I-94 (or successor form), or the 
 16273  expiration date noted on the EAD (Form I-766 or successor form) plus 
 16274  the 30-day departure period, as applicable, to prepare for departure 
 16275  from the United States, or to otherwise maintain status, including 
 16276  timely filing an EOS application in accordance with 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7) 
 16277  and 8 CFR 214.1 or to timely file a change of status application in 
 16278  accordance with 8 CFR 248.1(a). See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v). DHS 
 16279  removed the reference to completing a course of study or a program in 
 16280  order to provide consistency in the admission of all F-1 and J-1 
 16281  nonimmigrants and to allow the departure period to be reflected in I-94 
 16282  at admission, so that the F-1 and J-1 nonimmigrants will have a 
 16283  unambiguous end date of their period of authorized admission, easily 
 16284  referenced on the I-94. USCIS, when adjudicating applications for a 
 16285  change of status to F-1 and J-1 nonimmigrant status and EOS 
 16286  applications of F-1 and J-1 status will similarly provide I-797 
 16287  approval notices reflecting the 30-day departure period following the 
 16288  program end date or the 4-year maximum period of admission, or period 
 16289  of OPT or STEM OPT, as applicable.
 16290      In the final rule, DHS added a clarifying sentence to address 
 16291  situations where F-1 students end their study or training early. For 
 16292  example, an F-1 student may enter their program anticipating it will 
 16293  take 4 years to complete, but they may then complete that program in 3 
 16294  years. Or an F-1 student may enter their program anticipating it will 
 16295  take 4 years to complete, but they may stop their studies completely 
 16296  after one semester. When an F-1 student ends their study or training 
 16297  early, that student, and any eligible dependents, must, within 30 days 
 16298  from the new end date, depart the United States or otherwise seek to 
 16299  maintain lawful status. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v).
 16300      Since an F-1 student now has 30 days, rather than the previously 
 16301  allotted 60 days, to depart the country or to otherwise maintain status 
 16302  after their completion of their program or program end date, it follows 
 16303  that they need to file a Form I-765 or successor form for post-
 16304  completion OPT within 30 days, rather than the previously allotted 60 
 16305  days, after their program end date. See new 8 CFR 
 16306  214.2(f)(11)(i)(B)(2). This has been retained in the final rule.
 16307      It similarly follows that a student may not request a start date of 
 16308  OPT employment which is more than 30 days (rather than 60 days) after 
 16309  the student's program end date. DHS overlooked this update to 8 CFR 
 16310  214.2(f)(11)(i)(D) in the NPRM but has made the change in the final 
 16311  rule. As explained in the response to comments above, DHS recognizes 
 16312  failing to make this update may cause confusion. This technical change 
 16313  aligns with the 30-day period that was proposed in the NPRM under 8 CFR 
 16314  214.2(f)(11)(i)(B)(2) and with the 30-day period of preparation for 
 16315  departure under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v).
 16316      In the NPRM, DHS also proposed retaining the current regulatory 
 16317  language that allows a 15-day period for departure from the United 
 16318  States if an alien is authorized by the DSO to withdraw from classes, 
 16319  but no additional time for departure if the alien fails to maintain a 
 16320  full course of study without the approval of the DSO or otherwise fails 
 16321  to maintain status. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v). Because DSOs 
 16322  generally authorize withdrawal based on compelling academic or medical 
 16323  circumstances when a student proactively requests permission, DHS 
 16324  believes retaining the 15-day period is appropriate and has retained 
 16325  this provision in the final rule. However, aliens who fail to maintain 
 16326  their full course of study, are denied EOS, or
 16327  
 16328  [[Page 45106]]
 16329  
 16330  otherwise violate their status are required to immediately depart the 
 16331  United States, as is consistent with other nonimmigrant 
 16332  classifications. DHS considered allowing a short ``grace period'' for 
 16333  departure after an EOS denial but concluded there was not a compelling 
 16334  reason to treat F nonimmigrants who have received a denial more 
 16335  favorably than other nonimmigrant classifications. As in other 
 16336  nonimmigrant classifications, failure to immediately depart under these 
 16337  circumstances may result in accrual of unlawful presence and subject 
 16338  the individual to removal.
 16339  4. Automatic Extension of Authorized Period of Stay and Employment
 16340  a. Authorized Period of Stay and Employment Authorization Under 8 CFR 
 16341  214.2(f)(5)(viii)
 16342      Each year, a number of U.S. employers seek to employ F-1 students 
 16343  and file a Form I-129, Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker, with USCIS, 
 16344  along with a change of status request, to obtain classification of the 
 16345  F-1 student as an H-1B nonimmigrant worker. The H-1B nonimmigrant visa 
 16346  program allows U.S. employers to temporarily employ foreign workers in 
 16347  specialty occupations, defined by statute as occupations that require 
 16348  the theoretical and practical application of a body of highly 
 16349  specialized knowledge and a bachelor's or higher degree in the specific 
 16350  specialty, or its equivalent. See INA sections 101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b) and 
 16351  214(i); 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b) and 1184(i). The H-1B 
 16352  classification, however, is subject to annual numerical allocations, 
 16353  commonly referred to as a ``cap.'' See INA sections 214(g)(1)(A) and 
 16354  (g)(5)(C); 8 U.S.C. 1184(g)(1)(A) and (g)(5)(C).\323\ For purposes of 
 16355  the H-1B numerical allocations, each fiscal year begins on October 1. 
 16356  Petitioners may not file H-1B petitions more than 6 months before the 
 16357  date of actual need for the employee.\324\ Thus, the earliest date an 
 16358  H-1B cap-subject petition may be filed for an allocation for a given 
 16359  fiscal year is April 1, 6 months prior to the start of the applicable 
 16360  fiscal year for which initial H-1B classification is sought.
 16361  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16362  
 16363      \323\ Under INA 214(g)(1)(A), 8 U.S.C. 1184(g)(1)(A), 65,000 
 16364  aliens may be issued H-1B visas or otherwise provided H-1B 
 16365  nonimmigrant status in a fiscal year. This limitation does not apply 
 16366  to aliens who have earned a master's or higher degree from a U.S. 
 16367  institution of higher education, as defined in 20 U.S.C. 1001(a), 
 16368  until the number of aliens who are exempted from such numerical 
 16369  limitation during such year exceeds 20,000. INA 214(g)(5)(C), 8 
 16370  U.S.C. 1184(g)(5)(C).
 16371      \324\ See 8 CFR 214.2(h)(2)(i)(I).
 16372  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16373  
 16374      Many F-1 students complete a program of study or post-completion 
 16375  OPT in mid-spring or early summer. Per existing regulations, after 
 16376  completing their program or post-completion OPT, F-1 students have 60 
 16377  days (which DHS is proposing to change to 30 days) to take the steps 
 16378  necessary to maintain legal status or depart the United States. See new 
 16379  8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v). However, because the change to H-1B status cannot 
 16380  occur until October 1, an F-1 student whose program or post-completion 
 16381  OPT expires in mid-spring has two or more months following the 60-day 
 16382  period before the authorized period of H-1B status can commence. To 
 16383  address this situation, commonly known as the ``cap-gap,'' DHS 
 16384  established regulations that automatically extended F-1 D/S and, if 
 16385  applicable, post-completion OPT employment authorization for certain F-
 16386  1 nonimmigrants until April 1 of the fiscal year for which the H-1B 
 16387  status is being requested or until the validity start date of the 
 16388  approved petition, whichever is earlier. See redesignated 8 CFR 
 16389  214.2(f)(5)(vii). The extension of F-1 D/S and OPT employment 
 16390  authorization is commonly known as the ``cap-gap extension.'' This rule 
 16391  does not change the ``cap-gap extension'' provisions; it simply removes 
 16392  the reference to D/S and makes clear that an automatic extension will 
 16393  be granted to those with a fixed period of stay.
 16394  b. F-1 Status and Authorized Employment While EOS and/or Employment 
 16395  Authorization Applications Are Pending
 16396      DHS struck ``duration of status'' from redesignated 8 CFR 
 16397  214.2(f)(5)(vii) in the proposed rule and clarified that an alien with 
 16398  F-1 status whose admission period as indicated on his or her I-94 has 
 16399  expired, but who has timely filed an EOS application, will be 
 16400  authorized to continue pursuing a full course of study after the end 
 16401  date of his or her admission until USCIS adjudicates the EOS 
 16402  application. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii). This change allows for 
 16403  ongoing authorization to continue studies as long as the student has 
 16404  timely filed his or her EOS and will not penalize students if USCIS is 
 16405  unable to adjudicate an EOS application before a student's new term or 
 16406  course of study is underway. In such cases, students will be able to 
 16407  continue pursuing their full course of study.\325\ This change is 
 16408  retained in the final rule.
 16409  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16410  
 16411      \325\ However, if the extension of stay application is received 
 16412  during the 30-day period under new paragraph 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v), 
 16413  the F-1 student is authorized to continue a full course of study but 
 16414  may not continue or begin engaging in practical training or other 
 16415  employment. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B).
 16416  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16417  
 16418      DHS did clarify the title of new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii) in the 
 16419  final rule, since the automatic extension is for the authorized period 
 16420  of stay while the EOS is adjudicated, rather than an automatic EOS. The 
 16421  title changed from ``Automatic Extension of F stay and employment 
 16422  authorization. . .'' to ``Automatic extension of the authorized period 
 16423  of stay and employment authorization. . .''
 16424      The shift to a fixed date of admission has implications for various 
 16425  types of employment authorization. Prior to the effective date of this 
 16426  final rule, DSOs could authorize certain types of employment 
 16427  authorization, including on-campus employment and CPT,\326\ and 
 16428  students generally did not need to be concerned about a specific 
 16429  expiration date for their student status, and thus their employment 
 16430  authorization, because they were admitted for D/S. This rule changes 
 16431  that framework with different implications for various types of 
 16432  employment authorization.
 16433  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16434  
 16435      \326\ See 8 CFR 214.2(f)(9)-(12), 8 CFR 274a.12(b)(6)(iv).
 16436  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16437  
 16438      For on-campus employment where no EAD is needed, DHS is allowing 
 16439  aliens in F-1 status to continue to be authorized for on-campus 
 16440  employment while their EOS applications with USCIS are pending, not to 
 16441  exceed a period of 240 days.\327\ See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii). If 
 16442  the EOS application is still pending after 240 days have passed, the F-
 16443  1 student will no longer be authorized for employment and will need to 
 16444  stop engaging in on-campus employment. DHS is allowing a 240-day 
 16445  automatic extension period in order to minimize disruptions to on-
 16446  campus employment by teaching assistants, post-graduates working on 
 16447  research projects, and other positions that are integral to an F-1 
 16448  student's educational program. Note that the 240 days start after the 
 16449  expiration of one's current stay. DHS has always encouraged and will 
 16450  continue to encourage all nonimmigrants to apply for EOS within
 16451  
 16452  [[Page 45107]]
 16453  
 16454  the six months \328\ preceding the expiration of their current 
 16455  authorized stay thereby providing an additional buffer against any 
 16456  disruption of the ability to work.
 16457  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16458  
 16459      \327\ See 8 CFR 214.2(f)(9)(i) for a description of on-campus 
 16460  employment. For on-campus employment that is based on severe 
 16461  economic hardship resulting from emergent circumstances pursuant to 
 16462  redesignated 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(vi), see later discussion for 
 16463  additional restrictions. The EOS application must be timely filed 
 16464  pursuant to the new paragraph at 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B). 
 16465  Moreover, if an F-1 student files an extension of stay application 
 16466  during the 30-day period provided in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v)(new), he 
 16467  or she does not receive an automatic extension of authorized 
 16468  employment, including on-campus, CPT, and severe economic hardship, 
 16469  and must wait for approval of the extension of stay application (and 
 16470  employment authorization application, if required) before engaging 
 16471  in CPT or employment. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii).
 16472      \328\ With respect to the earliest filing date for a Form I-539, 
 16473  there is no prohibition on filing the form before a certain date 
 16474  ahead of expiration.
 16475  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16476  
 16477      Likewise, DHS is allowing an automatic extension of off-campus 
 16478  employment authorization for up to 240-days during the pendency of the 
 16479  EOS application, for F-1 students who have demonstrated severe economic 
 16480  hardship pursuant to 8 CFR 214.2(f)(9)(ii)(C) and previously received 
 16481  an EAD from USCIS that expired at the program end date that is now 
 16482  being extended with the EOS application. See new 8 CFR 
 16483  214.2(f)(5)(viii). These circumstances may include loss of financial 
 16484  aid or on-campus employment without fault on the part of the student, 
 16485  substantial fluctuations in the value of currency or exchange rate, 
 16486  inordinate increases in tuition and/or living costs, unexpected changes 
 16487  in the financial condition of the student's source of support, medical 
 16488  bills, or other substantial and unexpected expenses. In such cases, DHS 
 16489  believes a 240-day automatic extension of employment authorization will 
 16490  help alleviate the severe economic hardship and avoid a disruption in 
 16491  their employment, especially given the fact that an EAD is required and 
 16492  the frequency at which these students must submit an application for 
 16493  employment authorization.\329\ Additionally, given that USCIS's average 
 16494  EAD processing time is typically 60-120 days for foreign students and 
 16495  90-120 for most others, a 240-day timeframe provides sufficient 
 16496  flexibility in case of unexpected delays.
 16497  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16498  
 16499      \329\ See 8 CFR 274a.12(c)(3). 8 CFR 214.2(f)(9)(ii)(F)(2) 
 16500  provides that employment authorization based upon severe economic 
 16501  hardship may be granted in one-year intervals up to the expected 
 16502  date of completion of the student's current course of study.
 16503  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16504  
 16505      For F-1 students granted off-campus employment authorization on the 
 16506  basis of severe economic hardship resulting from emergent circumstances 
 16507  pursuant to redesignated 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(vi), DHS proposed, and is 
 16508  retaining in the final rule, an automatic extension of such employment 
 16509  authorization with a different validity period than the general 8 CFR 
 16510  214.2(f)(9)(ii)(C) severe economic hardship employment authorization 
 16511  extension described above while their EOS applications are pending. See 
 16512  new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii). This will codify USCIS's current policy 
 16513  which states USCIS may grant SSR employment authorization for the 
 16514  duration of the Federal Register notice validity period, but the period 
 16515  of authorization may not exceed the F-1 student's academic program end 
 16516  date.\330\
 16517  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16518  
 16519      \330\ See generally USCIS Policy Manual, Vol. 2, Part F, Chap. 
 16520  6, Employment, https://www.uscis.gov/policy-manual/volume-2-part-f-chapter-6 (last visited Feb. 4, 2026).
 16521  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16522  
 16523      As first promulgated in 1998, the SSR regulations provide necessary 
 16524  flexibility to address unforeseeable emergencies by allowing DHS, by 
 16525  notice in the Federal Register, to suspend the applicability of some or 
 16526  all of the requirements for on- and off-campus employment authorization 
 16527  for specified F-1 students where an emergency situation has arisen 
 16528  calling for this action. These F-1 students must continue to attend 
 16529  classes but are allowed to take a reduced course load. By regulation, 
 16530  aliens approved for SSR to take at least 6 semester or quarter hours of 
 16531  instruction at the undergraduate level or 3 semester or quarter hours 
 16532  of instruction at the graduate level. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v). 
 16533  Failure to take the required credits could be considered a failure to 
 16534  maintain F-1 status. The SSR regulations are announced by notice in the 
 16535  Federal Register, and such employment may only be undertaken during the 
 16536  validity period of the SSR notice.
 16537      Due to the shift to a fixed admission period, DHS proposed to 
 16538  provide an automatic extension of SSR-based employment so aliens' 
 16539  ability to benefit from this long-standing regulatory relief is not 
 16540  interrupted by USCIS processing times. This change is consistent with 
 16541  current USCIS policy, which allows for SSR employment authorization to 
 16542  be granted for the duration of the Federal Register notice validity 
 16543  period, so long as the period of authorization may not exceed the F-1 
 16544  student's academic program end date. It is also consistent with 
 16545  existing practice for certain nonimmigrants who require an EAD.\331\ 
 16546  This is retained in the final rule. Further, DHS has retained its 
 16547  proposal to automatically extend SSR authorization if an F-1 student 
 16548  has a timely-filed EOS pending for up to the end date stated in the 
 16549  Federal Register notice announcing the suspension of certain 
 16550  requirements, or 240 days, whichever is earlier. See new 8 CFR 
 16551  214.2(f)(5)(viii).
 16552  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16553  
 16554      \331\ See 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)-(12), 8 CFR 274a.12(b)(6)(iv).
 16555  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16556  
 16557      As evidence of these automatic extensions of employment 
 16558  authorization, DHS will allow the F-1 student's I-94 (or successor 
 16559  form) or EAD (Form I-766, or successor form), for F-1 nonimmigrants 
 16560  requiring an EAD, when combined with a notice issued by USCIS 
 16561  indicating receipt of a timely filed EOS application (such as the Form 
 16562  I-797),\332\ to be considered unexpired until USCIS issues a decision 
 16563  on the EOS application, not to exceed 240 days. See new 8 CFR 
 16564  214.2(f)(5)(viii). SSR-based employment authorization that has been 
 16565  automatically extended can be evidenced by the F-1 student's EAD and 
 16566  the receipt notice issued by USCIS (the Form I-797), not to exceed the 
 16567  lesser of 240 days or the end date stated in the Federal Register 
 16568  notice announcing the suspension of certain requirements.
 16569  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16570  
 16571      \332\ However, if an F-1 student files an extension of stay 
 16572  application during the 30-day period provided in new paragraph 8 CFR 
 16573  214.2(f)(5)(v), he or she does not receive an automatic extension of 
 16574  authorized employment, including on-campus, CPT, and severe economic 
 16575  hardship, and must wait for approval of the extension of stay 
 16576  application (and employment authorization application, if required) 
 16577  before engaging in CPT or employment. 214.2(f)(5)(viii).
 16578  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16579  
 16580  5. New Process for EOS Application
 16581      Under current regulations, F-1 students may obtain a program 
 16582  extension from a DSO as long as they are maintaining status and making 
 16583  normal progress toward the completion of their educational objectives. 
 16584  See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(i) and (iii). The problem with the ``normal 
 16585  progress'' standard is that it is undefined, and DHS believes that 
 16586  retaining it could lead to inconsistent adjudications. Even now, the 
 16587  lack of a standard definition for normal progress leads DSOs to 
 16588  inconsistently extend F-1 students' program end dates and thus their 
 16589  stay in the United States. Some DSOs use a strict standard, evaluating, 
 16590  for example, documentation to support a student's claim of a compelling 
 16591  medical condition or illness that serves as the basis for the student's 
 16592  request for extension of the student's current program. However, other 
 16593  DSOs claim that the student is making ``normal progress'' whenever a 
 16594  student simply needs more time to complete the program. This 
 16595  inconsistency results in some students being able to remain in F-1 
 16596  status for years simply by having the DSO update the Form I-20 without 
 16597  providing a justification as to how the student is making ``normal 
 16598  progress'' and what academic or medical circumstances necessitate the 
 16599  extension of the program.
 16600      Therefore, DHS proposed not to use a ``normal progress'' standard 
 16601  with respect to seeking a program extension, and to require, in 
 16602  addition to the requirement that the applicant obtain a Form I-20 from 
 16603  the DSO recommending extension of the program, the applicant will be 
 16604  required to file an EOS
 16605  
 16606  [[Page 45108]]
 16607  
 16608  application to request additional time to complete their current course 
 16609  of study beyond their authorized period of admission. See new 8 CFR 
 16610  214.2(f)(7)(i). This change is retained in the final rule.
 16611      Apart from pursuing a new course of study, DHS appreciates that the 
 16612  time for study can legitimately fluctuate given the changing goals and 
 16613  actions of the student. For example, a student may experience 
 16614  compelling academic or medical reasons, or circumstances beyond their 
 16615  control that cause them to need additional time in the United States 
 16616  beyond the predetermined end date of the program in which they were 
 16617  initially enrolled. DHS understands these circumstances arise and 
 16618  believes these scenarios present an appropriate situation for DHS to 
 16619  directly evaluate the nonimmigrant's eligibility for additional time in 
 16620  the United States. However, instead of effectively extending their stay 
 16621  through a DSO's program extension recommendation in SEVIS, students 
 16622  will have to obtain a Form I-20 from the DSO recommending a program 
 16623  extension and apply to USCIS for an EOS. Immigration officers thereby 
 16624  will be able to conduct appropriate background and security checks on 
 16625  the applicant at the time of the EOS application and directly review 
 16626  the proffered evidence to ensure that the alien is eligible for the 
 16627  requested EOS, including through assessing whether the alien remains 
 16628  admissible. See 8 CFR 214.1(a)(3)(i). This extra step is necessary 
 16629  because an immigration officer will be able to see a more fulsome 
 16630  picture while considering the student's particular circumstances, and 
 16631  be able to identify potential fraud and criminality, thereby ensuring 
 16632  public safety and program integrity.
 16633      In these circumstances, DHS will only extend the stay beyond the 
 16634  program end date of an otherwise eligible F-1 student requesting 
 16635  additional time to complete their program if the additional time needed 
 16636  is due to a compelling academic reason, documented medical illness or 
 16637  medical condition, or circumstance that was beyond the student's 
 16638  control. As with all nonimmigrant EOS requests, an alien seeking an EOS 
 16639  generally must have continually maintained status.\333\ If an F-1 
 16640  student dropped below a full course of study, that drop must have been 
 16641  properly authorized. F-1 students seeking extensions of stay must 
 16642  primarily be seeking to temporarily stay in the United States solely to 
 16643  pursue a full course of study, INA section 101(a)(15)(F)(i), 8 U.S.C. 
 16644  1101(a)(15)(F)(i), and not for other reasons separate from, or in
