 16646  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16647  
 16648      \333\ Failure to file on or before the expiration of the 
 16649  previously accorded status or failure to maintain such status may be 
 16650  excused at the discretion of USCIS if the alien demonstrates that at 
 16651  the time of filing: the delay was due to extraordinary circumstances 
 16652  beyond the control of the applicant, and USCIS finds the delay 
 16653  commensurate with the circumstances, the alien has not otherwise 
 16654  violated his or her status, and is not subject to deportation. See 8 
 16655  CFR 214.1(c)(3)(viii).
 16656  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16657  
 16658      If an F-1 student were to violate the terms of his or her F-1 
 16659  status, the F-1 student would need to apply to USCIS for reinstatement, 
 16660  consistent with 8 CFR 214.2(f)(16). If a student is reinstated and his 
 16661  or her admit until date expires within 6 months, but the student is 
 16662  unable to complete his or her program of study within that time, then 
 16663  the F-1 student also would need to apply to USCIS for an EOS. In that 
 16664  scenario, the F-1 student would need to make separate requests for 
 16665  reinstatement and for EOS by submitting a separate form for each 
 16666  request, including the required filing fee for each form, by marking 
 16667  reinstatement on one form and then EOS on the other. Both forms can 
 16668  then be submitted together at the same time to avoid unnecessary 
 16669  adjudication delays. In the event both forms are submitted together, 
 16670  and the F-1 student's application to reinstate student status is 
 16671  denied, his or her application for EOS would also be denied, with both 
 16672  filing fees being retained by USCIS and not refunded.
 16673      By way of illustration, a student with a fixed date of admission 
 16674  may request an additional 4 months to complete his or her program 
 16675  because the student was authorized to drop below a full course of study 
 16676  for one semester due to illness. Prior to the effective date of this 
 16677  final rule, the student would need to request an updated Form I-20 from 
 16678  the DSO recommending a program extension. Now, consistent with the 
 16679  proposal in the NPRM, an immigration officer could review the proffered 
 16680  evidence and ensure that the claim is supported by documentation from a 
 16681  medical doctor. Conversely, a student may request an EOS for additional 
 16682  time to complete an associate program but fail to submit evidence they 
 16683  were properly authorized to drop below a full course of study. The 
 16684  immigration officer has discretion to request transcripts from the 
 16685  student. If a student's transcripts reflect that the student failed 
 16686  multiple classes one semester, an immigration officer could determine 
 16687  if the student has failed to maintain status due to a failure to carry 
 16688  a full course of study as required. In another example, a student could 
 16689  submit an EOS request to continue in the same program because he or she 
 16690  was unable to take all the required classes for his or her major due to 
 16691  over-enrollment at the school. Again, an officer could request 
 16692  additional information, if needed, to determine that the student was 
 16693  maintaining a full course of study (or, if not, was properly authorized 
 16694  to reduce his or her course load), but due to the school's high 
 16695  enrollment, the student may validly require an additional semester to 
 16696  complete the degree requirements in order to graduate.
 16697      Therefore, DHS proposed to eliminate a reference to ``normal 
 16698  progress'' with respect to seeking a program extension, and incorporate 
 16699  a new standard clarifying that acceptable reasons for requesting an 
 16700  extension of a stay for additional time to complete a program are: (1) 
 16701  compelling academic reasons; (2) a documented illness or medical 
 16702  condition; or (3) exceptional circumstances beyond the control of the 
 16703  alien. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(i)(C).\334\ These provisions are 
 16704  retained in the final rule.
 16705  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16706  
 16707      \334\ DHS did not propose to update the term ``normal progress'' 
 16708  as defined in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(6)(i)(E). The provision at 8 CFR 
 16709  214.2(f)(6)(i)(E) relates to study at an approved private elementary 
 16710  or middle school or public or private academic high school. In that 
 16711  context, it is clear that ``normal progress'' is the completion of 
 16712  the academic year (for example, 6th grade).
 16713  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16714  
 16715      The first two factors are based on the current regulatory 
 16716  provisions for program extension, 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii), from the 2025 
 16717  text (e.g., changes of major or research topics, and unexpected 
 16718  research problems). DHS proposed to clarify that, in addition to 
 16719  academic probation and suspension, a student's repeated inability or 
 16720  unwillingness to complete his or her course of study, as demonstrated 
 16721  by a pattern of failing classes and requesting multiple program 
 16722  extension, is not an acceptable reason to request an EOS for additional 
 16723  time to complete a program. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(i)(C)(1). This is 
 16724  also retained in the final rule.
 16725      DHS expects bona fide students to be committed to their studies, 
 16726  attending classes as required, carrying a full course of study, and 
 16727  making reasonable efforts toward program completion. Repeatedly failing 
 16728  classes demonstrates that the student is not making reasonable efforts 
 16729  toward completing his or her program of study. Therefore, a student who 
 16730  has a pattern of failing classes that has resulted in multiple program 
 16731  extensions would not be qualified for an EOS. The prohibition against 
 16732  requesting an EOS would not include students, such as those who, 
 16733  pursuant to DHS regulations, are making normal progress toward 
 16734  completing their program of study and still may not complete the 
 16735  program within 4 years
 16736  
 16737  [[Page 45109]]
 16738  
 16739  due to the standard timeline and requirements for the program. Absent 
 16740  such factors as being placed on academic probation or suspension, or 
 16741  repeatedly failing classes, these students would be eligible for 
 16742  extension based upon compelling academic reasons. This prohibition also 
 16743  does not include cases where the DSO properly authorized the student to 
 16744  drop below a full course of study as well as cases in which the status 
 16745  has been reinstated following a loss of status. In such case, the 
 16746  student is eligible for reinstatement if the reduced course load was 
 16747  within the DSO's power to authorize. A student would be expected to 
 16748  provide evidence demonstrating the compelling academic reason in order 
 16749  for the DSO to recommend a program extension. The student may then 
 16750  apply for an EOS. While a letter from the student may be sufficient to 
 16751  meet his or her burden of proof, an immigration officer will evaluate 
 16752  the individual case and make the determination as to whether additional 
 16753  evidence (such as a letter from a member of the school administration 
 16754  or faculty) is needed to adjudicate the case.
 16755      DHS also proposed to clarify that a student can qualify for a 
 16756  program extension and corresponding EOS based on a documented illness 
 16757  or medical condition. To provide an objective standard, DHS proposed to 
 16758  codify standards already included in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(6)(iii)(B), which 
 16759  requires a student to provide medical documentation from a licensed 
 16760  medical doctor, licensed doctor of osteopathy, licensed psychologist, 
 16761  or licensed clinical psychologist to substantiate the illness or 
 16762  medical condition if seeking a reduced course load. See new 8 CFR 
 16763  214.2(f)(7)(i)(C)(2). This is retained in the final rule. As this is 
 16764  already a long-standing requirement for DSOs and students in a similar 
 16765  context, DHS believes this will be appropriate and easy to implement in 
 16766  the program extension and corresponding EOS process. Further, requiring 
 16767  applicants to provide documentation of their medical illness or medical 
 16768  condition that caused their program delay is a reasonable request, 
 16769  because they are asking DHS to provide them additional time in the 
 16770  United States.
 16771      DHS also proposed a new factor in the EOS provisions--circumstances 
 16772  beyond the student's control, including a natural disaster, a national 
 16773  health crisis, or the closure of an institution. See new 8 CFR 
 16774  214.2(f)(7)(i)(C)(2)(iii). This is retained in the final rule. As in 
 16775  the reinstatement context, DHS believes that there might be additional 
 16776  reasons beyond compelling academic or documented medical reasons that 
 16777  result in a student's inability to meet the program end date listed on 
 16778  the Form I-20.
 16779      Therefore, DHS proposed a third prong that encompasses scenarios 
 16780  that are not envisioned in the current provisions governing the 
 16781  extension of a program end date, such as those noted above. Some 
 16782  scenarios are currently in the reinstatement provisions, 8 CFR 
 16783  214.2(f)(16)(i)(F), such as natural disasters, pandemics, and the 
 16784  negligence of a DSO, and DHS believes that they merit favorable 
 16785  consideration in extension requests moving forward. Other scenarios may 
 16786  present circumstances that require a more intensive, fact-specific 
 16787  analysis and may fall into this proposed third prong. For example, the 
 16788  circumstances surrounding the closure of a school may be considered in 
 16789  determining whether the student qualifies for an EOS. By way of 
 16790  illustration, if a school closes as a result of a criminal conviction 
 16791  of its owners for engaging in student visa fraud by not requiring 
 16792  students to attend, but the student is unable to demonstrate that he or 
 16793  she was attending classes prior to closure as required to fulfill a 
 16794  full course of study, the closure of the institution might not qualify 
 16795  the student for a program extension. In contrast, if a school closes 
 16796  but a student is able to demonstrate that he or she was attending 
 16797  classes and was fulfilling all requirements to otherwise remain in 
 16798  status, the closure of the institute may qualify the student for a 
 16799  program extension.
 16800      The requirements to timely request an extension of the program end 
 16801  date would remain largely unchanged; however, DHS proposed a technical 
 16802  change to replace all references to the DSO ``granting'' an extension 
 16803  of the program with the term ``recommend'' an extension of the program 
 16804  in order for the student to file for EOS because USCIS, not the DSO, 
 16805  would ``grant'' the EOS. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(ii). This is 
 16806  retained in the final rule. For example, a student may not necessarily 
 16807  be granted an EOS by USCIS if an adjudicator determines the student has 
 16808  not actually maintained status or does not actually have compelling 
 16809  academic or documented medical reasons for the delay, despite the DSO's 
 16810  recommendation for program extension.
 16811      Where the alien requests a recommendation to extend the program end 
 16812  date, the DSO could only make a recommendation to extend the program if 
 16813  the alien requested the extension before the program end date noted on 
 16814  the most recent Form I-20, or successor form. Additionally, consistent 
 16815  with changes throughout this rule, once the DSO recommends the 
 16816  extension of the program, the alien would need to timely file for an 
 16817  EOS on the form and in the manner designated by USCIS, with the 
 16818  required fees and in accordance with the filing instructions, including 
 16819  any biometrics required by 8 CFR 103.16 and a valid, properly endorsed 
 16820  Form I-20 or successor form, showing the new program end date barring 
 16821  extraordinary circumstances. See 8 CFR 214.1(c)(4) and new 8 CFR 
 16822  214.2(f)(7)(ii) and (f)(7)(iii). This is retained in the final rule.
 16823      If seeking an EOS to engage in any type of practical training, the 
 16824  alien in F-1 status will also need to have a valid Form I-20, properly 
 16825  endorsed for practical training, and be eligible to receive the 
 16826  specific type of practical training requested. See new 8 CFR 
 16827  214.2(f)(7)(v). This is retained in the final rule. Finally, as with 
 16828  all immigration benefit requests, an immigration officer will generally 
 16829  not grant an EOS where an alien in F-1 status failed to maintain his or 
 16830  her status.
 16831      Finally, a student's failure to timely request, from the DSO, a 
 16832  recommendation for extension of the program end date prior to 
 16833  expiration of the student's authorized stay, which would result in the 
 16834  DSO recommending an extension of the program end date in SEVIS after 
 16835  the end date noted on the most recent Form I-20 or successor form, will 
 16836  require the alien to file for a reinstatement of F-1 status, because 
 16837  the alien will have failed to maintain status and will be ineligible 
 16838  for an EOS. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(viii). A request for 
 16839  reinstatement must be filed in the manner and on the form designated by 
 16840  USCIS, with the required fee, including any biometrics required by 8 
 16841  CFR 103.16. DHS is also requiring F-2 dependents seeking to accompany 
 16842  the F-1 principal student to file applications for an EOS or 
 16843  reinstatement, as applicable. These requirements are consistent with 
 16844  current provisions.
 16845      With the transition from D/S to admission for a fixed time period, 
 16846  F-1 students will need to apply for an EOS directly with USCIS, by 
 16847  submitting the appropriate form and following the requirements outlined 
 16848  in the form instructions. USCIS anticipates accepting the Form I-539, 
 16849  Application to Change/Extend Nonimmigrant Status, for this population 
 16850  but would like the flexibility to use a new form if more efficient or 
 16851  responsive to workload needs. Thus, DHS is retaining its proposal to 
 16852  use general language to account for a possible change in form in
 16853  
 16854  [[Page 45110]]
 16855  
 16856  the future. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(A). If the form ever 
 16857  changes, USCIS would provide stakeholder's advance notice on its web 
 16858  page and comply with Paperwork Reduction Act requirements.
 16859      Like all other aliens who file a Form I-539, F-1 applicants may be 
 16860  required to submit biometrics and may be required to appear for an 
 16861  interview pursuant to 8 CFR 103.2(b)(9). In addition, applicants will 
 16862  need to demonstrate that they are eligible for the nonimmigrant 
 16863  classification sought. Accordingly, applicants must submit evidence of 
 16864  sufficient funds to cover expenses. A failure to provide such evidence 
 16865  will render the applicant ineligible for the EOS. See new 8 CFR 
 16866  214.2(f)(7)(ii).
 16867      While the sponsoring school is required to verify the availability 
 16868  of financial support before issuing the Form I-20, they may not be 
 16869  well-versed in foreign documentation submitted by applicants and 
 16870  circumstances may change between the issuance of a Form I-20 and a 
 16871  request for an EOS. Further, it is incumbent upon DHS to determine the 
 16872  veracity of the evidence submitted, and officers must ensure that the 
 16873  student has sufficient funds to study in the United States without 
 16874  resorting to unauthorized employment. The phrase ``sufficient funds to 
 16875  cover expenses'' is referred to in existing DoS regulations concerning 
 16876  issuance of F and M nonimmigrant student visas, 22 CFR 41.61(b)(1)(ii), 
 16877  and current DoS policy requires an applicant to provide documentary 
 16878  evidence that sufficient funds are, or will be, available to defray all 
 16879  expenses during the entire period of anticipated study.\335\ While this 
 16880  does not mean that the applicant must have cash immediately available 
 16881  to cover the entire period of intended study, which may last several 
 16882  years, the applicant must demonstrate enough readily available funds to 
 16883  meet all expenses for the first year of study and that additional funds 
 16884  will be available for the duration of the intended period of 
 16885  study.\336\ DHS believes requiring evidence of readily available 
 16886  financial resources to cover expenses for one year of study is 
 16887  reasonable given that F students are familiar with this requirement 
 16888  because this is the standard used by the DoS in the issuance of F 
 16889  nonimmigrant visas. DHS also considers that this standard is 
 16890  appropriate because it establishes concrete resources for one full 
 16891  academic year of the program. Further, applicants must demonstrate 
 16892  that, barring unforeseen circumstances, adequate funds will be 
 16893  available for each subsequent year of study from the same source or 
 16894  from one or more other specifically identified and reliable financial 
 16895  sources. Such evidence for one year and subsequent years could include, 
 16896  but is not limited to: complete copies of detailed financial account 
 16897  statements for each account intended to be used to fund the student's 
 16898  education; other immediately available cash assets; receipts and/or a 
 16899  letter from the school accounts office indicating tuition payments 
 16900  already made and any outstanding account balance; affidavits of support 
 16901  from a sponsor; proof of authorized private student loans; \337\ and/or 
 16902  other financial documentation.
 16903  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16904  
 16905      \335\ See 9 FAM 402.5-5(G), Adequate Financial Resources, 
 16906  https://fam.state.gov/FAM/09FAM/09FAM040205.html (last updated Aug. 
 16907  15, 2024).
 16908      \336\ Id.
 16909      \337\ Federal student loans are only available to U.S. citizens 
 16910  and permanent residents.

 16914  application--meaning that USCIS will need to receive the application on 
 16915  or before the date the authorized admission period expires. See new 8 
 16916  CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B). This application timeframe for timely filing 
 16917  an EOS application will include the 30-day period of preparation for 
 16918  departure allowed after the completion of studies or any authorized 
 16919  practical training. However, if the extension application is received 
 16920  during the 30-day period of preparation for departure provided in 8 CFR 
 16921  214.2(f)(5)(v) following the completion of studies, the alien in F-1 
 16922  status may continue studying but may not continue or begin engaging in 
 16923  practical training or other employment until the extension request is 
 16924  approved and, as applicable, an EAD is issued. See new 8 CFR 
 16925  214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B). To avoid this scenario, DHS continues to encourage 
 16926  nonimmigrants to file their EOS applications within the six months 
 16927  \338\ preceding the expiration of their stay.
 16928  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16929  
 16930      \338\ With respect to the earliest filing date for a Form I-539, 
 16931  there is no prohibition on filing the form before a certain date 
 16932  ahead of expiration.
 16933  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16934  
 16935      The length of the extension granted could be up to the period of 
 16936  time needed to complete the program or requested practical training, 
 16937  not to exceed 4 years, unless the alien is a border commuter, enrolled 
 16938  in language training, or attending a public high school. By permitting 
 16939  admission only ``up to'' the prescribed period, USCIS and CBP are 
 16940  afforded discretion as to the ultimate length of time to grant the 
 16941  applicant and consider factors such as program length.
 16942      F-2 dependents seeking to accompany the F-1 principal student will 
 16943  need to file applications for an EOS or reinstatement, as applicable. 
 16944  See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iv). A dependent F-2 spouse and unmarried 
 16945  children under the age of 21 seeking to accompany the principal F-1 
 16946  student during the additional period of admission will need to either 
 16947  be included on the primary applicant's request for extension or 
 16948  properly file their own EOS applications on the form designated by 
 16949  USCIS. If the dependent files a separate Form I-539, he or she will 
 16950  need to pay a separate Form I-539 filing fee. However, if the dependent 
 16951  files a Form I-539A as part of the primary applicant's EOS request on a 
 16952  Form I-539, only one fee will be required.
 16953      USCIS generally will need to receive the extension applications on 
 16954  or before the expiration of the previously authorized period of 
 16955  admission, including the 30-day period following the completion of the 
 16956  course of study, as indicated on the F-2 dependent's I-94. To qualify 
 16957  for an EOS, the F-2 dependent will need to demonstrate the qualifying 
 16958  relationship with the principal F-1 student who is maintaining status, 
 16959  also be maintaining his or her own status, and not have engaged in any 
 16960  unauthorized employment. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iv). Extensions of 
 16961  stay for F-2 dependents will not be able to exceed the authorized 
 16962  admission period of the principal F-1 student. By removing D/S for 
 16963  family members, DHS is ensuring that a spouse who engaged in 
 16964  unauthorized employment would be denied EOSs and must return home. As 
 16965  with other nonimmigrant classifications, if a dependent is aging out 
 16966  before the program end date listed on the I-20, the entire family, 
 16967  including the J-1 principal, will receive an EOS only until the F-2's 
 16968  21st birthday, which will then require the remaining family members and 
 16969  the principal F-1 student to apply for an EOS for the remainder of the 
 16970  program and for the aged out F-2 to leave the country or change status 
 16971  to a different nonimmigrant category.
 16972      Under new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(vii), if USCIS denies the request for 
 16973  an extension, and the period of admission for the student and his or 
 16974  her dependents has expired, then the student and his or her dependents 
 16975  will need to immediately depart the United States. As with other 
 16976  nonimmigrant classifications, they will not be given any period of time 
 16977  to prepare for departure from the United States after the denial, and 
 16978  there may be significant immigration consequences for failing to depart 
 16979  the country immediately. For example, such aliens generally will begin 
 16980  to accrue unlawful presence the day after the issuance of the denial. 
 16981  DHS
 16982  
 16983  [[Page 45111]]
 16984  
 16985  believes this standard provides parity across nonimmigrant 
 16986  classifications.
 16987  6. School Transfers and Changes in Educational Objectives
 16988      The proposed rule discussed several examples of fraudulent ``pay-
 16989  to-stay'' schemes in which students were falsely reported as 
 16990  maintaining status in return for cash payments to DSOs.\339\ 
 16991  Furthermore, the D/S framework has enabled some aliens to become 
 16992  ``professional students'' who spend years enrolled in programs at the 
 16993  same educational level (for example, multiple associate degree 
 16994  programs) or complete programs at one educational level and enroll in 
 16995  lower educational levels (such as completing a master's degree and then 
 16996  enrolling in an associate program).\340\ While admission for a fixed 
 16997  time period will help to address these concerns, DHS proposed 
 16998  limitations on program changes within and between educational levels to 
 16999  further strengthen the integrity of the F nonimmigrant visa 
 17000  classification by better ensuring that aliens are in the United States 
 17001  primarily to study, rather than to reside permanently in the United 
 17002  States. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i). The final rule retains this 
 17003  provision.
 17004  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 17005  
 17006      \339\ 90 FR at 42094-95 (Aug. 28, 2025).
 17007      \340\ DHS analysis of data in SEVIS and valid as of May 7, 2025, 
 17008  and June 2, 2026.

 17010

 17012  change of educational level conditions. First, as is the case 
 17013  currently, aliens would need to begin classes at the transfer school or 
 17014  program within 5 months of transferring out of the current school or 
 17015  within 5 months of the program completion date on his or her current 
 17016  Form I-20; and second, if the alien is authorized to engage in post-
 17017  completion or STEM OPT, he or she must be able to begin or resume 
 17018  classes within 5 months of transferring out of the school that 
 17019  recommended OPT or the date the OPT authorization ends, whichever is 
 17020  earlier. This is retained in this final rule, although, as compared the 
 17021  NPRM, the regulatory text in the final rule replaces the statement that 
 17022  the F-1 student ``must be able to resume classes within 5 months. . .'' 
 17023  with the F-1 student ``must be able to begin or resume classes within 5 
 17024  months . . .''. See new CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(G) and (H).

content.text:
**Optimizing Token Usage**

I'm focusing now on maximizing token efficiency. My current goal is to refine `fr_text` and `fr_grep` calls for the remaining budget, ensuring each one delivers the highest possible yield. I'm aiming for concise, impactful operations within `2026-14439`.

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".
query.title: Query

doc_type.description: Document types: RULE, PRORULE (proposed rule), NOTICE, PRESDOCU (presidential document). null for all.
doc_type.title: Doc Type

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.
agency.title: Agency

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).
pres_type.title: Pres Type

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

**Examining Limitations**

I've been poring over the fine print, and a potential sticking point leaps out at me from lines 8131-8134 in the Federal Register (91 FR 45039). The document states students with extenuating circumstances such as illness will be limited to the original 24-month admission period. This is an unexpected limitation, isn't it?


**Analyzing Regulations**

I'm now diving into the specifics of the regulations. I've pinpointed a contradiction between `8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(vi)` and `8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)(A)`, with the latter restricting English Language Training (ELT) students to a strict 24-month period, seemingly overriding other extensions. The preamble, at multiple points within the Federal Register, reinforces this limitation, even in extenuating circumstances. It looks like I've clarified **Q15 #4**. Now to move on to transfer processes and fees.

  8455  schools or changing majors after the first year of study is allowed at

  8460      This particular change seeks to address significant costs incurred 
  8461  by universities when working with potential F-1 students who then 
  8462  transfer to less expensive schools upon arrival in the United States. 
  8463  This provision will provide more stability in the admission process and 
  8464  still provides the students with the ability to explore coursework and 
  8465  majors during the first year. Most undergraduate students take similar 
  8466  classes in their first year; therefore, the majority of the commenters' 
  8467  objections about changing degrees in the first year are not a concern 
  8468  under this new framework.
  8469  f. Program Changes for Graduate Students
  8470      Comments: Commenters stated that changes to graduate programs do 
  8471  not account for actual experiences of students. The majority of 
  8472  commenters expressed opposition to the proposed rule's prohibition on 
  8473  F-1 graduate students changing programs or educational objectives 
  8474  during their program of study. Commenters expressed particular concern 
  8475  about the impact on Ph.D. students, remarking that the proposed 
  8476  restrictions demonstrate a lack of understanding about the nature of 
  8477  graduate education, which often involves interdisciplinary work and 
  8478  evolving research interests.
  8479      Commenters stated that the rule would disrupt common practices in 
  8480  graduate education, including master's students being promoted to Ph.D. 
  8481  programs midway through their studies, Ph.D. students receiving 
  8482  master's degrees enroute to their doctorate, and students pursuing dual 
  8483  degrees at the graduate level. Another commenter expressed the proposed 
  8484  rule would eliminate the ``master-out'' option for Ph.D. students who 
  8485  are awarded a master's degree when they cannot finish, and harm 
  8486  ``academic mobility'' for second master's degrees and master's-out 
  8487  pathways. Commenters clarified that graduate school, particularly at 
  8488  the doctoral level, is not a fixed, linear path, and intellectual 
  8489  discovery often leads students to pivot to related fields. Commenters 
  8490  stated that the rule would punish academic growth by causing students 
  8491  to abandon years of work rather than transition programs. Many 
  8492  commenters expressed concern with the proposed rule's different 
  8493  provisions for graduate students compared to undergraduate students, 
  8494  noting that the proposed rule lacks explanation or rationale for these 
  8495  distinctions. One commenter reported extenuating and uncontrollable 
  8496  circumstances may cause a graduate student to transfer programs or 
  8497  institutions, while another commenter thought the proposed rule would 
  8498  punish students for issues beyond their control by locking students 
  8499  into a major their first year and by requiring graduate students to 
  8500  remain in their program. Another commenter stated that the proposed 
  8501  rule would make Ph.D. enrollment riskier and would leave open teaching 
  8502  assistant and research positions that are dependent on foreign 
  8503  students.
  8504      Commenters provided numerous reasons why graduate students might 
  8505  need to change programs, including refined research direction, changes 
  8506  in advisors, moves from master's to doctoral programs, suggestions from 
  8507  faculty members, personal or academic circumstances, and changes in 
  8508  research funding. Commenters emphasized the critical relationship 
  8509  between graduate students and their faculty advisors, explaining that 
  8510  students often choose specific institutions because of faculty members 
  8511  whose research aligns with their interests, reasoning that when faculty 
  8512  members relocate to another university, graduate students may need to 
  8513  transfer to continue working with their chosen mentors and maintain 
  8514  access to specialized research facilities. Commenters noted that 
  8515  research funding is often tied to specific faculty members, requiring 
  8516  students to follow their advisors to maintain financial support.
  8517      Commenters urged DHS to reconsider its restrictions on graduate 
  8518  students seeking to transfer or change educational objectives, with 
  8519  specific requests to allow Ph.D. students the option to transfer, 
  8520  particularly in cases involving academic or financial necessity. If DHS 
  8521  proceeds with finalizing the rule, commenters suggested establishing 
  8522  exceptions, such as allowing students to transfer to continue 
  8523  mentorship with their advisor, and proposed simplifying procedures for 
  8524  program extensions and transfers, especially at the graduate level. 
  8525  Commenters asked what happens after the 240-day authorized stay ends 
  8526  while an application is pending, the earliest filing date for 
  8527  applications, and how Ph.D. students whose programs exceed four years 
  8528  would justify extensions.
  8529      Commenters noted the rule could prevent individuals who completed a 
  8530  Ph.D. from later enrolling in a U.S. MD program or vice versa, despite 
  8531  these degrees preparing students for distinct career paths. Commenters 
  8532  expressed concern about uncertainty for medical residents on F-1 visas 
  8533  regarding whether residency would be considered a higher education 
  8534  level than medical school, potential barriers to changing disciplines 
  8535  during residency, and disruptions to transitions between PharmD 
  8536  programs or movement from PharmD to research-focused graduate programs.
  8537      Relatedly, a few commenters noted that the changes would prohibit 
  8538  students from pursuing a second master's degree which could hamper 
  8539  their ability to shift careers and add interdisciplinary training. One 
  8540  commenter pursuing a second STEM master's degree also expressed concern 
  8541  for the uncertainty surrounding using OPT after a second master's 
  8542  degree and stated that this might direct students away from the United 
  8543  States. Another commenter spoke about how the inability to pursue a 
  8544  second master's degree may hamper a student from ``applied, industry-
  8545  ready training.''
  8546      Response: DHS acknowledges that students may seek to engage in 
  8547  programs simultaneously at a lower level or obtain multiple degrees, at 
  8548  differing levels, throughout the course of their time in the United 
  8549  States. Students will be able to continue earning such credentials 
  8550  while also making progress in the degree program for which they have 
  8551  been issued a Form I-20. For example, a student issued a Form I-20 for 
  8552  a Ph.D. program as their primary academic objective could obtain a 
  8553  master's degree incidental to
  8554  
  8555  [[Page 45043]]
  8556  
  8557  status while progressing toward completion of the Ph.D. program.
  8558      DHS generally relies on NCES' definition of educational levels, 
  8559  which provides a structure for determining whether a nonimmigrant 
  8560  student's program of study reflects upward academic progression. The 
  8561  list of educational levels that schools use to update their Form I-17, 
  8562  ``Petition for Approval of School for Attendance by Nonimmigrant 
  8563  student,'' is available at https://studyinthestates.dhs.gov/sevis-help-hub/school-records/school-certification/form-i-17-listing-of-available-degrees. This list contains the following educational levels: 1. 
  8564  Primary and Secondary Education; 2. ELT; 3. Post-secondary 
  8565  Certificates/Non-Degree; 4. Associate; 5. Bachelor; 6. Master; 7. 
  8566  Doctorate. DHS may provide updated guidance on educational levels to 
  8567  ensure consistency across components and with ED.
  8568      DHS appreciates commenters' concerns about the rule's effect on 
  8569  academic growth of students. DHS recognizes academic pathways can be 
  8570  complex and that students may pursue multiple degrees or transition 
  8571  programs, including from undergraduate to graduate studies. The 
  8572  Department does not intend to discourage academic advancement or 
  8573  require students to abandon years of work.
  8574      DHS also recognizes the different approaches for undergraduate 
  8575  students and graduate students. This rule aims to balance program 
  8576  integrity and national security with the need to support legitimate 
  8577  educational pursuits. DHS believes differing approaches for 
  8578  undergraduate and graduate students are appropriate given the 
  8579  difference in the general ages of the students, a graduate student's 
  8580  previous opportunities to explore academic interests prior to entering 
  8581  graduate school, and a focus on more specific degree programs at the 
  8582  graduate level. DHS maintains it is appropriate to prohibit an F-1 
  8583  student at the graduate degree level or above from changing educational 
  8584  objectives at any point during their program of study for the reasons 
  8585  outlined above. However, DHS recognizes that extenuating circumstances, 
  8586  such as a school closure or a school's prolonged inability to hold in-
  8587  person classes due to a natural disaster, may prevent a graduate 
  8588  student from being able to continue their studies unless the student 
  8589  transfers to another SEVP-certified institution. The NPRM proposed 
  8590  prohibiting an F-1 student at the graduate level from transferring, 
  8591  without exception. DHS agrees with commenters that these situations may 
  8592  be outside the students' control and, taking this into consideration, 
  8593  DHS has amended the regulatory text to allow SEVP to authorize an 
  8594  exception to this transfer prohibition in extenuating circumstances. 
  8595  See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A), 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(C), and 8 CFR 
  8596  214.2(f)(8)(i)(D). For the purposes of this rule, ``extenuating 
  8597  circumstances'' for a transfer are rare, exceptional events beyond the 
  8598  control of the school and the affected students that prevent an SEVP-
  8599  certified school from continuing to provide the student's approved 
  8600  course of study, such as a permanent or extended school closure, a 
  8601  school merger that eliminates the student's program, a loss of 
  8602  necessary authorization for the school to enroll F-1 students, or the 
  8603  school's prolonged inability to deliver required instruction due to a 
  8604  natural disaster or comparable emergency. In such circumstances, SEVP 
  8605  may, in its discretion and in coordination with the impacted SEVP-
  8606  certified school or schools, permit the transfer of student records to 
  8607  another SEVP-certified school so that the student may continue, to the 
  8608  extent practicable, in the same educational objective. This exception 
  8609  is narrow, is intended only to preserve continuity of study in 
  8610  emergency situations, does not create an entitlement to transfer, and 
  8611  does not otherwise authorize an F-1 student to change educational 
  8612  objectives. Affected students generally will access this exception 
  8613  through their DSOs, as SEVP becomes aware of qualifying extenuating 
  8614  circumstances through notifications from SEVP-certified schools and 
  8615  SEVP's existing outreach to schools during such events.
  8616      Regarding the claim that the rule will make Ph.D. enrollment 
  8617  riskier and result in unfilled teaching assistant and research 
  8618  positions, DHS does not intend for this rule to significantly affect 
  8619  these populations since foreign students may still study, teach, and 
  8620  research in the United States under this fixed period of admission 
  8621  framework. They may also apply for an EOS if they want to request an 
  8622  extension of their admission period and shouldn't experience any 
  8623  disruptions if they apply as early as possible (180 days) before the 
  8624  expiration of their current stay. Additionally, assistantships are 
  8625  awarded based on student need and should not be the primary motivation 
  8626  in enrolling foreign students.
  8627      Regarding comments on the relationship between graduate students 
  8628  and their faculty advisors and students choosing institutions based on 
  8629  faculty member's research, such students should consider applying for 
  8630  J-1 visas to better align their goals with the appropriate nonimmigrant 
  8631  status. DHS notes that J-1 categories include research scholars and 
  8632  college and university students, and requirements for transferring 
  8633  programs for J-1 students are governed by DoS regulations. See 22 CFR 
  8634  62.20, 62.23, 62.42.
  8635      DHS also acknowledges the request for simplified procedures for 
  8636  program extensions and transfers. DHS declines to alter the current 
  8637  procedures, as they are necessary for program integrity and national 
  8638  security. DHS will, however, evaluate needs for guidance to assist in 
  8639  the transition and application of these new rules and will provide this 
  8640  guidance to stakeholders as needed.
  8641      DHS recognizes commenters' request for clarification about what 
  8642  happens after the 240-days. The 240-day period offers certain F 
  8643  nonimmigrants the ability to continue with authorized employment for 
  8644  this time period while their EOS is pending. If the EOS takes longer 
  8645  than 240 days to adjudicate, the F nonimmigrant would need to stop 
  8646  authorized employment, but they can remain in the United States, can 
  8647  continue their full course of study, and are considered to be in a 
  8648  period of authorized stay during that period.
  8649  g. Delay and Suspension of Change in Educational Objectives
  8650      Comment: Commenters discussed several technical and implementation 
  8651  concerns regarding the proposed limitations on program changes and 
  8652  transfers. A commenter expressed concern that the discretionary 
  8653  provision in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(E) may be exploited by future 
  8654  administrations. Other commenters opined DHS should not codify a 
  8655  regulation which cannot be implemented. Another commenter opined the 
  8656  delay or suspension of the educational objectives provision could 
  8657  create confusion and arbitrary outcomes. Similarly, a commenter thought 
  8658  8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(E) would cause students, schools, and employers 
  8659  unnecessary uncertainty and resulting harm.
  8660      Response: DHS recognizes that this rule requires updates to SEVIS 
  8661  and other systems and it has been planning for these changes. The 
  8662  language proposed in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(E) would provide DHS 
  8663  authority to delay or suspend implementation of the provisions relating 
  8664  to a change in educational objectives, outlined in 8 CFR 
  8665  214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A) through (C), via announcement in the Federal 
  8666  Register and SEVP's website. DHS has given the comments on this 
  8667  provision considerable thought and agrees that this provision, as 
  8668  proposed, could cause unnecessary confusion and uncertainty
  8669  
  8670  [[Page 45044]]
  8671  
  8672  in the future. DHS does not identify an indefinite need to suspend or 
  8673  delay the implementation of 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(A) through (C) and 
  8674  therefore, DHS has decided to amend 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(E) to limit the 
  8675  agencies' ability to delay or suspend implementation to two years from 
  8676  the effective date of this final rule.
  8677  2. Preparation for Departure
  8678  a. Support for Reducing the F-1 Departure Period From 60 to 30 Days
  8679      Comments: A few commenters expressed support to reduce the F-1 visa 
  8680  departure period from 60 days to 30 days. One commenter stated the 60-
  8681  day departure period was misaligned with enforcement objectives and 
  8682  increased the risk of visa overstays. This commenter referenced DHS 
  8683  reports showing above-average overstay rates in the student and 
  8684  exchange visitor visa categories. Another commenter stated that 
  8685  shortening the departure period would limit the risk of unauthorized 
  8686  employment or ``loitering'' after the lawful stay has ended.
  8687      Response: DHS appreciates the commenters' support for this rule and 
  8688  agrees that reducing the departure period will reduce overstays, 
  8689  strengthen oversight, and yield additional benefits to enhance the U.S. 
  8690  immigration system. This rule establishes an effective mechanism to 
  8691  periodically and directly assess whether nonimmigrants in F, J, and I 
  8692  status are complying with the conditions of their nonimmigrant 
  8693  classifications and U.S. immigration laws, and to obtain timely and 
  8694  accurate information about the activities these aliens have engaged in 
  8695  and plan to engage in during their temporary stay in the United States. 
  8696  DHS believes that this rule will encourage aliens to maintain lawful 
  8697  status and reduce instances in which aliens in F, J, and I nonimmigrant 
  8698  status unlawfully remain in the United States after their program, 
  8699  practical training, or activities or assignments end.
  8700  b. Opposition to Reducing the F-1 Departure Period From 60 to 30 Days
  8701      Comments: Most commenters expressed opposition to reducing the F-1 
  8702  post-completion departure period from 60 to 30 days for many reasons 
  8703  because this timeframe serves as a critical buffer for foreign students 
  8704  in transitioning without risking life-changing immigration penalties 
  8705  for minor issues at no fault of the alien before going back to their 
  8706  country. For example, commenters said delayed transcripts, job offers, 
  8707  or cancelled or delayed flights could trigger unlawful presence which 
  8708  could lead to bans from re-entering the U.S. Commenters also remarked 
  8709  that DHS presented no data suggesting the current 60-day period poses 
  8710  national security issues or compromises program integrity. As one 
  8711  commenter stated, there is no evidence offered that the extra 30 days 
  8712  are somehow used to threaten national security, avoid authorities, or 
  8713  otherwise abuse the F-1 visas. Another commenter stated that the 
  8714  shortening of the grace period from 60 to 30 days was unnecessary and 
  8715  counterproductive to ensure an orderly completion of stay.
  8716      Commenters stated that 30 days was insufficient for foreign 
  8717  students to complete post-graduation logistics such as terminating 
  8718  housing leases, selling belongings, closing financial accounts, 
  8719  arranging shipping, and making travel arrangements. Commenters added 
  8720  that these unresolved logistical and financial matters often burden 
  8721  local communities when students cannot efficiently conclude their 
  8722  affairs. In addition, commenters state a shortened 30-day departure 
  8723  period amid USCIS processing delays could lead to an increase in 
  8724  inadvertent overstays and unlawful presence, potentially exposing 
  8725  students to serious immigration consequences including reentry bans.
  8726      Commenters cited a negative impact on academic institutions, 
  8727  including an increased administrative burden for schools and DSOs, who 
  8728  would face greater pressure to process requests quickly in the 30-day 
  8729  grace period during already busy periods, potentially leading to higher 
  8730  error rates.
  8731      One commenter stated the shortened departure period will negatively 
  8732  impact foreign students in transition to other institutions or 
  8733  educational levels. Regarding academic transitions, a commenter stated 
  8734  that many institutions require more than 30 days to post final grades,

 13470  
 13471      \275\ Based on Supporting Statement for Form I-539 values, 24.5 
 13472  percent of F-1, J-1, and I applicants (70% paper applicants * 35%

 13475  
 13476      Comments: One commenter criticized the cost analysis for the 
 13477  biometrics appointments required as part of the EOS process. The

 13492  will incur different travel costs based on location and availability of 
 13493  transportation; they were included in the regulatory impact analysis of

 13495  same experience for all nonimmigrants. Some will incur small costs due 
 13496  to proximity and low-cost transportation, and others will incur higher 
 13497  costs. This figure is meant to provide an average per nonimmigrant but 
 13498  will not be the specific cost for all nonimmigrants.

 13501  and uncertainty associated with international travel, exiting and

 13514  impact analysis for the NPRM and Final Rule, DHS assumes that, while 
 13515  requesting an EOS at a POE is an option, many nonimmigrants wishing to 
 13516  remain in the country will file an EOS and remain in country instead of 
 13517  incurring costs due to travel and reentry. The regulatory impact 
 13518  analysis also assesses how the impacts would change if nonimmigrants 
 13519  sought extensions while traveling through a POE instead of filing the 
 13520  I-539 or I-539A form.

 13523  unquantifiable and intangible costs associated with the uncertainty of 
 13524  applying for a new period of admission. These include (1) the lack of 
 13525  published adjudication data for Form I-539 to inform the likelihood of 
 13526  EOS denial under the proposed rule, (2) current processing time issues 
 13527  at the USCIS California Service Center, which reports an average of 4.5 
 13528  months for changes to F-1 or J-1 status and 3.5 months for extensions,

 13531  losing their money.

 13533  interruption in a student's studies. However, any such denial would be 
 13534  warranted due to an applicant's lack of eligibility for an EOS (i.e.,

 13536  fails classes, failed to maintain their nonimmigrant status, or has a 
 13537  criminal history).

 13539  have occurred due to various factors not related to this rulemaking. 
 13540  DHS believes that factors contributing to this backlog will not be 
 13541  present when more significant influx of EOS applications resulting from 
 13542  this final rule are anticipated to be filed with USCIS. USCIS, as a fee 
 13543  funded agency, may set fees to support the additional workload 
 13544  associated with adjudication of cases subject to section 212(a)(4) of 
 13545  the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(4). USCIS conducts comprehensive fee studies 
 13546  on a biennial basis to assess whether its fee schedule adequately 
 13547  accounts for the full cost of naturalization and adjudication services. 
 13548  This assessment necessarily takes into account the projected volume of 
 13549  filings and the level of effort necessary to adjudicate various 
 13550  immigration benefit requests.\276\ USCIS will allocate appropriate 
 13551  levels of resources to ensure the adjudication of EOS continues in a 
 13552  timely fashion. Due to the expected growth of fees paid for the I-539 
 13553  form, USCIS will have more resources to allocate to meet the demand.

 13556      \276\ USCIS published a rule to change its fee schedule. See 
 13557  USCIS Fee Schedule and Changes to Certain Other Immigration Benefit 
 13558  Request Requirements, 85 FR 46788 (Aug. 3, 2020), corrected by USCIS 
 13559  Fee Schedule and Changes to Certain Other Immigration Benefit 
 13560  Request Requirements, 85 FR 49941 (Aug. 17, 2020) (Fee Rule). The

 13568  petitions.

 13570  
 13571      Students will be aware of their allowed length of stay as well as 
 13572  the end date for their length of stay. Students who do not wish to

 13587  cases. USCIS conducts comprehensive fee studies on a biennial

 13590  
 13591  basis to assess whether its fee schedule adequately accounts for the 
 13592  agency's full costs. Additionally, the regulatory impact analysis for 
 13593  this rule qualitatively assesses how USCIS requests for additional 
 13594  information or in-person interviews may impose additional costs on 
 13595  USCIS.

 13597  the economic and operational impact of the proposed rule on USCIS, 
 13598  despite the agency potentially needing to process hundreds of thousands 
 13599  of additional EOS applications. Without evidence, these comments stated 
 13600  that USCIS currently lacks the necessary systems, staffing, training, 
 13601  information technology (IT) infrastructure, and integration 
 13602  capabilities to manage such an increase in application volume 
 13603  efficiently. One commenter highlighted that USCIS is already facing 
 13604  significant resource constraints and processing delays, particularly 
 13605  after the recent loss of experienced personnel due to government 
 13606  downsizing and added that further workload increases without adequate 
 13607  resources would likely strain the agency and lead to longer processing 
 13608  times. Another commenter recommended that DHS fully assess the 
 13609  potential impact of the proposed rule on application processing times

 13613  in fee-paying volumes of EOS applications received by USCIS following

 13616  However, DHS notes that the most significant increase in the volume of 
 13617  EOS applications will not materialize until 4 years after the effective 
 13618  date of this rule. This will allow time for DHS to shift resources as 
 13619  needed and as appropriate to ensure that the larger increased volumes 
 13620  are integrated into existing workflows. Several commenters noted and 
 13621  DHS has acknowledged backlogs in the processing of EOS applications. 
 13622  DHS believes that, given that 80 percent of Form I-539 adjudications 
 13623  for F, M, and J aliens are completed in three months,\277\ factors 
 13624  contributing to this backlog will not be present when the EOS 
 13625  applications resulting from this final rule are anticipated to be filed 
 13626  with USCIS. The fees collected with the increase in applications will 
 13627  result in additional resources for USCIS to use to mitigate the impact 
 13628  on the processing queue. The funds can be used to allocate appropriate 
 13629  resources to ensure adjudication of the I-539 in a timely manner. This 
 13630  will lessen the impact on processing times for applications with USCIS.
 13631  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 13632  
 13633      \277\ DHS, USCIS, Case Processing Times, https://egov.uscis.gov/processing-times/ (last accessed Feb. 23, 2026).

 13637  the regulatory impact analysis. According to Circular A-4 guidance on

 13641  rule which DHS is unable to effectively quantify, DHS elects to

content.text:
**Analyzing Adjudication Timelines**

I've been examining lines 13622-13624, specifically focusing on the reported adjudication times for Form I-539. It seems DHS believes that 80% of these cases are resolved within three months. This timeframe is crucial and will be factored into the present considerations of the overall EOS (end of service).

  5462  personal plans based on the longstanding D/S policy. The Department 
  5463  carefully considered these reliance interests during the rulemaking 
  5464  process. In developing the final rule, DHS sought to minimize 
  5465  disruption by including a transition period, mechanisms for extensions 
  5466  of stay, and clear guidance for students and school officials. These 
  5467  measures are intended to provide affected individuals and institutions 
  5468  with sufficient time and flexibility to adjust to the new requirements.
  5469      I nonimmigrants will also have sufficient preparation time with the 
  5470  60-day effective date in this rule and the transition provisions in new 
  5471  8 CFR 214.1(m)(3). Any I nonimmigrants who are properly maintaining 
  5472  their status on the date this rule takes effect and who were admitted 
  5473  for D/S are authorized to remain in the United States in I nonimmigrant 
  5474  status for a period necessary to complete their activity, not to exceed 
  5475  either 90 or 240 days (with the shorter period for those I 
  5476  nonimmigrants with a passport from the PRC (except for Hong Kong SAR 
  5477  and Macau SAR passport holders)). See new 8 CFR 214.1(m)(3). The 90- or 
  5478  240-days period is not calculated until the rule takes effect. Id. If 
  5479  an alien needs additional time, they may be able to stay in the United 
  5480  States longer in I nonimmigrant status by filing an EOS with USCIS in 
  5481  accordance with new 8 CFR 214.1(c)(2) and new 8 CFR 214.2(i)(5).
  5482  2. Clarity and Guidance for Transition Cases
  5483      Comments: Commenters sought clarification for cases where a 
  5484  student's Form I-20 is no longer valid on the effective date of the 
  5485  rule, or where SEVIS records are terminated or pending updates. They 
  5486  requested assurance that students are not deemed unlawfully present due 
  5487  to technical or timing issues beyond their control. A commenter 
  5488  requested clarification about how unlawful presence will be accrued for 
  5489  aliens transitioning from D/S to a fixed period of stay.
  5490      Response: An F-1 student whose program or OPT has ended on the 
  5491  effective date of the rule will have the remainder of their allowed 
  5492  departure period to leave the United States, i.e., 60 days from the 
  5493  program end date on their I-20. See new 8 CFR 214.1(m). Students 
  5494  needing additional time will not be subject to the transition provision 
  5495  but rather be subject to the new rule and must apply for an EOS. SEVP 
  5496  will continue to process SEVIS corrections as needed. Students should 
  5497  not remain in the United States with a terminated or completed SEVIS 
  5498  record beyond their allowed departure period. Under this final rule, 
  5499  aliens who remain in the United States beyond a fixed time period 
  5500  generally will begin accruing unlawful presence. Calculation of accrual 
  5501  of unlawful presence resulting from the elimination of D/S under this 
  5502  rule will not be applied retroactively but for those with completed 
  5503  programs and therefore expired I-20, unlawful presence will be begin to 
  5504  accrue on the effective date of the rule unless they have applied for 
  5505  reinstatement, a change or status, or an EAD for OPT or STEM OPT before 
  5506  the effective date of the rule. In addition, this rule will not take 
  5507  effect until September 15, 2026, it includes a transition period for 
  5508  nonimmigrants who are currently on D/S, and it allows nonimmigrants to 
  5509  remain lawfully in the United States while an EOS is pending. These 
  5510  provisions will mitigate any issues which may arise related to 
  5511  technical or timing issues beyond their control. Unlawful presence will 
  5512  start to accrue for those on D/S when the nonimmigrant fails to comply 
  5513  with the terms of their F, J, or I nonimmigrant category, or when they 
  5514  fail to transition to admission under a fixed period of time within the 
  5515  time allotted for in new 8 CFR 214.1(m).
  5516  
  5517  [[Page 45018]]
  5518  
  5519  3. Lack of Clarity and System Modifications
  5520      Comments: Commenters expressed confusion about the transition 
  5521  period's impact on various student scenarios, status end dates, and the 
  5522  interplay between SEVIS, I-94s, and USCIS systems. They requested clear 
  5523  instructions, updated documents, and system improvements to track 
  5524  status and avoid errors.
  5525      Response: DHS believes the transition provision is clear: students 
  5526  in D/S status on the rule's effective date continue their programs, 
  5527  only needing to apply for EOS if their program exceeds the program end 
  5528  date on their DS-2019 or I-20, or 4 years after the effective date of 
  5529  the rule, whichever comes first. This addresses various student 
  5530  scenarios. For the EOS adjudication, SEVIS information is used by USCIS 
  5531  officers as part of their adjudication process to determine 
  5532  eligibility. Travel abroad during the transition period triggers 
  5533  conversion to the fixed-date regime. Upon admission following their 
  5534  travel, students will receive an I-94 with a fixed date. DHS is in the 
  5535  process of completing updates to SEVIS to incorporate this new rule and 
  5536  updates will include information about the end date from the Form I-94. 
  5537  USCIS, CBP, DoS, and ICE have always had and will continue to have 
  5538  access to necessary information from each other. DHS and DoS will 
  5539  provide any necessary updated instructions, guidance, and training to 
  5540  stakeholders, including DSOs and ROs, and will ensure technical updates 
  5541  are completed prior to the effective date. DHS and DoS websites will be 
  5542  updated as needed to inform F-1 and J-1 participants about how to 
  5543  maneuver the new system.
  5544  4. Modifications to Transition Period
  5545      Comments: Commenters proposed additional support during the 
  5546  transition, such as streamlined extensions, clear guidance, training, 
  5547  funding for DSOs, and phased implementation. Suggestions included 
  5548  robust grace periods, service standards, digital filings, reasonable 
  5549  fees, and expedited lanes for academic deadlines. Some commenters 
  5550  warned that too many exceptions increase confusion. Commenters also 
  5551  recommended detailed implementation guidance, technical assistance, and 
  5552  public education efforts. Similarly, a commenter wrote that the 
  5553  proposed rule should include specific procedures for the transition 
  5554  from D/S to fixed time period admission of authorized stay for F and J 
  5555  nonimmigrants.
  5556      Response: DHS appreciates the suggestions but declines to make 
  5557  further modifications to the rule based on these suggestions. Many are 
  5558  already part of the transition period, such as current D/S holders 
  5559  remaining in D/S until their program or OPT ends. This transition 
  5560  period results in a phased implementation, since F, J, and I 
  5561  nonimmigrants can transition to admission for a fixed period of time 
  5562  over the course of the next four or so years. Additional grace periods 
  5563  are also not being adopted due to this transition period and the 
  5564  implementation period between the final rule's publication date and the 
  5565  rule's effective date, which is 60 days. DHS maintains that the 
  5566  transition provisions provide an appropriate mechanism for 
  5567  transitioning D/S nonimmigrants to a fixed period of time. DHS and DoS 
  5568  will provide guidance and training as needed, including training for 
  5569  DSOs and ROs to ensure a smooth transition. DHS will continue to 
  5570  evaluate its process for extensions and available technological 
  5571  improvements and appreciates commenters' desires for continued 
  5572  streamlining and digital filings. DHS also appreciates commenters' 
  5573  desire for additional funding of DSOs, but this is outside the scope of 
  5574  this rulemaking.
  5575  5. Transition Period for Specific Categories
  5576  a. F and J Nonimmigrants
  5577      Comments: Commenters stated that replacing D/S with fixed-date 
  5578  rules, coupled with transition rules and new limits, creates traps for 
  5579  diligent students and dependents, increases costs, and disrupts 
  5580  academic and professional progress. They expressed concern about the 
  5581  impact on family members and the risk of losing work authorization or 
  5582  facing school disruptions.

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty
