Q9.answer: Between the August 28, 2025 NPRM (**FR Doc. 2025-16554**, 90 FR 42070) and the July 17, 2026 Final Rule (**FR Doc. 2026-14439**, 91 FR 44976), DHS made the following F-1 changes (seven listed): **(1) Extenuating-circumstances exception to the graduate school-transfer ban:** The NPRM barred graduate-level F-1 students from transferring schools without exception; the final rule added authority for SEVP to authorize an exception for extenuating circumstances (e.g., school closure or prolonged inability to hold in-person classes due to natural disaster). *Final rule paragraphs:* **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A)** and **8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(C)** (91 FR 45125, 45127). *Described at:* Section IV.J.1.f (**91 FR 45043**), Section V.A (**91 FR 45097**), and Section V.F.2 (**91 FR 45104**). **(2) Two-year sunset and Federal Register notice requirement for delaying/suspending educational-objective limits:** The NPRM allowed DHS to delay or suspend 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A)–(C) indefinitely via SEVP's website; the final rule capped that authority at two years from the effective date (**until September 14, 2028**) and required publication of a **Federal Register notification** in addition to SEVP's website. *Final rule paragraph:* **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(E)** (91 FR 45125). *Described at:* Section II.C (**91 FR 44979**), Section IV.J.1.g (**91 FR 45043–45044**), Section V.A (**91 FR 45097**), and Section V.F.2 (**91 FR 45104–45105**). **(3) Shortening the maximum post-program window for a requested OPT start date from 60 to 30 days:** Fixing an omission in the NPRM, DHS replaced '60' with '30' so an F-1 student cannot request a post-completion OPT start date more than **30 days** after the program end date, aligning with the 30-day departure and OPT filing period. *Final rule paragraph:* **8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i)(D)** (91 FR 45124). *Described at:* Section V.A (**91 FR 45097**) and Section V.F.3 (**91 FR 45105**). **(4) Explicit 30-day departure rule upon *early* completion/cessation of study or training (and immediate departure upon status violation):** DHS added language requiring an F-1 student (and dependents) who ends study or training *prior* to expiration of the admission period to depart or seek to maintain lawful status within **30 days** of that end date, and stating that a student who fails to maintain a full course of study or status must **leave the country immediately**. *Final rule paragraph:* **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v)** (91 FR 45125). *Described at:* Section II.C (**91 FR 44979**), Section V.A (**91 FR 45097**), Section V.B (**91 FR 45098**), and Section V.F.3 (**91 FR 45105**). **(5) Express prospective date ('after September 15, 2026') in the same/lower educational level bar:** DHS inserted *'after September 15, 2026'* directly into the regulatory text so the bar on maintaining, being admitted in, or otherwise obtaining F-1 status at the same or a lower educational level applies only to programs completed after the rule's effective date (and changed 'F-1 nonimmigrant' to 'F-1 student'). *Final rule paragraph:* **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(C)** (91 FR 45125). *Described at:* Section V.A (**91 FR 45097**). **(6) Clarifying CBP readmission after travel as an alternative to a USCIS EOS for post-completion OPT:** DHS revised the post-completion OPT EOS paragraph to state explicitly that recommended students (outside the transition exemption) must apply for employment authorization and *either* apply for an EOS with USCIS *or* **seek admission through CBP after travel abroad**. *Final rule paragraph:* **8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(D)** (91 FR 45127). *Described at:* Section V.A (**91 FR 45097**). **(7) Clarifying public charter schools, K–12 school-progression transfers, post-OPT class starts, and D/S transition EOS/OPT structure:** DHS clarified that 'public high school' (12-month cap) may include **charter or similar taxpayer-funded schools** (**8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)(C)**, 91 FR 45124; described at **91 FR 45096, 45102**); added needing to change schools to complete elementary or secondary education as an extenuating-circumstances example (**8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A)**, 91 FR 45125; **91 FR 45097, 45104**); added 'first' before 'academic year' in **8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(D)** and 'begin or' before 'resume classes' after OPT in **8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(H)** (91 FR 45127; **91 FR 45097, 45111**); and clarified D/S transition EOS eligibility in **8 CFR 214.1(c)(3)(v)** and separated **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(iii)** into a standalone paragraph so DHS's 6-month extension authority covers all of (m)(1)(i)–(ii) (91 FR 45123; **91 FR 45097, 45100–45101**).

Q11.answer: **What the final rule (FR Doc. 2026-14439) says on EOS cost:** **(1) Final regulatory text:** Does **not** set or state a dollar filing fee; it requires remitting 'the required fees' / 'the appropriate fee' per USCIS form instructions (8 CFR 214.1(c)(2), 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(A), (iv), 91 FR 45122–45123, 45126). **(2) DHS preamble explanations:** Surprisingly, **DHS never prints the exact dollar USCIS Form I-539 filing fee anywhere in the final rule text**; instead, DHS cross-references Table 16 ('Applicant Unit Costs for Filing an EOS with USCIS') in the separate docketed Regulatory Impact Analysis (91 FR 45082), notes in footnote 276 that USCIS accepts 'current fees' following the 2020 Fee Rule injunction (91 FR 45083), and explains that including F-2 dependents on Form I-539A with the principal's Form I-539 requires **only one Form I-539 filing fee**, whereas filing a separate Form I-539 requires a separate fee (91 FR 45110). For auxiliary applicant burdens, DHS cites an average outside legal/preparer cost of **$490** assumed for **24.5%** of EOS filers (91 FR 45083), an average **50-mile round trip** for biometrics (91 FR 45083), and PRA time burdens of **1.667 hours** (paper Form I-539), **1.0 hour** (e-filed Form I-539), **0.35 hours** (Form I-539A), and **1.17 hours** (biometrics) (91 FR 45120; with total annualized EOS costs across F/J/I nonimmigrants estimated at $317.3M–$317.9M, 91 FR 45116). **(3) Commenter statements (not DHS authority):** Commenters cited a **$420** USCIS EOS filing fee (91 FR 45055; and $1,680 for four EOS filings at 91 FR 45082), '$367 to over $800' for J-1 au pair extensions including fees/biometrics (91 FR 45056), and **$750 to $3,000** for private legal representation (91 FR 45082). **What the final rule says on USCIS processing time:** **(1) DHS preamble explanations:** DHS states (citing USCIS Case Processing Times accessed Feb. 23, 2026) that **80 percent of Form I-539 adjudications for F, M, and J nonimmigrants are completed in 3 months** (91 FR 45084 & fn. 277), while repeatedly cautioning that **DHS cannot guarantee processing times** and that increased filing volume **may increase processing times** (91 FR 45009, 45021, 45025, 45029, 45031, 45052), and encouraging students to file up to **6 months (180 days)** before stay expiration (91 FR 45043, 45106–45107, 45110). *(DHS separately notes F-1 EAD processing times average 60–120 days, 91 FR 45032, 45107.)* **(2) Commenter statements (not DHS authority):** Commenters reported Form I-539 times of **~3.5 months** for extensions (and 4.5 months for COS at the California Service Center, 91 FR 44999, 45083), **more than 6.5 months** for 80% of EOS cases at Service Center Operations (91 FR 45063), **often exceeding 240 days** (91 FR 45031), and **6–19 months** or **12–18 months** during peak backlogs (91 FR 45031, 45036, 45048, 45051). **Draft informational text for the adviser's student handout:** *'Extending F-1 stay inside the United States requires filing Form I-539 with USCIS and paying USCIS's current Form I-539 filing fee (which also covers F-2 dependents included on Form I-539A at no extra filing fee; check USCIS's current fee schedule before filing, as the D/S final rule itself did not change or print the exact fee, though public comments noted a $420 fee). In the July 2026 final rule, DHS reported that USCIS completed 80% of F, M, and J Form I-539 applications within 3 months, but warned that processing times are not guaranteed and may lengthen, so DHS recommends applying up to 6 months (180 days) before your current stay expires.'*

Likewise, current real-time USCIS Form I-539 processing times as of November 2026 are published on USCIS's website rather than in the Federal Register.

Q12.answer: **(a) Is an I-539 received by USCIS during the 60 days after Priya's May 15, 2027 I-20 program end date (May 16–July 14, 2027) timely?** **Yes, under the best reading of the transition and EOS provisions—subject to two critical caveats (one substantive, one textual).** Because Priya was admitted for D/S and maintaining F-1 status on September 15, 2026, **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)** (final regulatory text) sets her authorized period of stay as her May 15, 2027 Form I-20 program end date **plus a 60-day departure period** (through **July 14, 2027**). Under **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B)**, an EOS application is timely filed if USCIS receives it *'on or before the date the authorized period of stay expires,'* and the preamble at **91 FR 45101** expressly confirms that D/S transition F-1 students must file an EOS request by their program end date *'plus an additional 60 days for F nonimmigrants.'* **Caveat 1 (SEVIS deadline for extending current program):** If Priya is extending her *current* bachelor's program (rather than transferring to a new master's program), **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(viii)** requires her DSO to have entered the program extension in SEVIS **on or before May 15, 2027**; if the DSO updates SEVIS after May 15, 2027, she is ineligible for an EOS and must apply for reinstatement. **Caveat 2 (Days 31–60 drafting gap):** In **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B)**, the explanatory clause after *'date the authorized period of stay expires'* says *'which includes the 30-day period provided in paragraph (f)(5)(v)'* without explicitly mentioning 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)'s 60-day transition period; thus days 1–30 (May 16–June 14, 2027) are completely ironclad, while days 31–60 (June 15–July 14, 2027) rely on reading 'authorized period of stay' together with 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1). **(b) Does she keep the automatic extension of on-campus or CPT employment if she files during those 60 days?** **No.** First, under **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)** (91 FR 45123), any authorized non-EAD employment or training for a D/S transition student **ends on the Form I-20 program end date** (May 15, 2027; see also 8 CFR 214.2(f)(9)(i) and (f)(10)(i), under which CPT and program-based on-campus employment cannot extend past program completion or the DSO's CPT end date on Form I-20). Second, **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii)** and **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B)** (91 FR 45126) explicitly bar any automatic extension of on-campus, CPT, or severe-economic-hardship employment when an EOS is filed during the post-program departure period: the student may continue full-time study, **but must wait for USCIS approval of the EOS before engaging in employment or CPT**. **Recommendation for the adviser:** Advise that if ongoing on-campus or CPT work eligibility is needed (assuming her academic program itself is continuing/extending), **the DSO must update SEVIS and USCIS must receive Form I-539 on or before May 15, 2027** (and DHS recommends filing up to 6 months early). If she is instead filing Form I-539 after May 15, 2027 (for instance, for her fall master's program or after a timely pre-May 15 SEVIS extension), she **must cease all on-campus and CPT work on May 15, 2027** and should strongly aim for USCIS receipt within the first **30 days** (**on or before June 14, 2027**) to avoid any adjudicator confusion over days 31–60.
Q12.basis: **Final regulatory text (FR Doc. 2026-14439):** 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1) (91 FR 45123, 60-day transition departure period and termination of authorized employment/training on Form I-20 program end date); 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v) and (viii) (91 FR 45125–45126, no automatic employment extension when EOS is filed during departure period, and CPT capped at DSO-authorized CPT end date); and 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B) and (viii) (91 FR 45126–45127, timely receipt on or before expiration of authorized stay, bar on employment when received during departure period, and reinstatement requirement if DSO enters SEVIS extension after Form I-20 end date). **Preamble explanation:** Section V.E.1 (91 FR 45101) and Section V.F.4–5 (91 FR 45106–45107 & fns. 325, 327, 332; 91 FR 45109–45110).
Q12.uncertainty: As noted in (a), 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B) defines timely filing by receipt 'on or before the date the authorized period of stay expires, which includes the 30-day period provided in paragraph (f)(5)(v),' omitting an explicit cross-reference to 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)'s 60-day transition departure period (even though 214.1(m)(1) and the preamble at 91 FR 45101 establish a 60-day authorized stay for transition F-1s). Similarly, 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii) refers to an F-1 student whose status 'as indicated on the Arrival/Departure Record, Form I-94 ... has expired,' whereas transition students hold 'D/S' I-94s; in any event, 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1) independently terminates non-EAD work authorization on the May 15, 2027 Form I-20 end date.

Q13.answer: **(a) Authorized stay after Sofia's January 9, 2027 return without filing anything:** **June 13, 2027.** Although Sofia was in the D/S transition group on September 15, 2026, departing the United States and re-entering after September 15, 2026 converts her to a **fixed period of admission** under **8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A)**, **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(ii)**, **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)**, and **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v)** (final regulatory text; preamble at 91 FR 45017, 45099, 45101). Upon her January 9, 2027 readmission, CBP admits her until her Form I-20 program end date (May 14, 2027, less than 4 years) **plus a 30-day departure period** (she loses the 60-day transition departure period). *Date arithmetic:* May 14, 2027 + 30 days = 17 remaining days in May (31 − 14 = 17, reaching May 31, 2027) + 13 days in June (30 − 17 = 13) = **June 13, 2027**. **(b) Whether she needs Form I-539 for OPT, and USCIS receipt deadline:** **Yes, she MUST file Form I-539** (in addition to Form I-765). Even though February 22, 2027 is on or before March 18, 2027, **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(ii)** explicitly provides that a D/S transition F-1 student **who departs the United States before filing the post-completion OPT application and is admitted with a fixed period of admission is required to file BOTH Form I-765 AND Form I-539** (see also 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(D), unless she travels again and is readmitted by CBP). Under **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B)** (and **8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i)(B)(2)**, which requires post-completion OPT filings within 30 days after the program end date and within 30 days of the DSO's SEVIS recommendation), USCIS must receive the Form I-539 **on or before June 13, 2027** (the expiration of her authorized stay; practically, she should file Form I-539 concurrently with Form I-765 on February 22, 2027—within 30 days of the DSO's SEVIS recommendation—so her stay and EAD can be approved by her June 10, 2027 OPT start date). *(Note: June 10, 2027 is 27 days after May 14, 2027 [17 days in May + 10 in June], within the 30-day maximum OPT start-date window in amended 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i)(D).)* **(c) Authorized stay if approved as requested (OPT through June 9, 2028):** **July 9, 2028.** Under **8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(D)** and **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v)** (and **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(vi)**), an approved OPT EOS includes a **30-day** departure period after the approved OPT end date. *Date arithmetic:* June 9, 2028 + 30 days = 21 remaining days in June (30 − 9 = 21, reaching June 30, 2028) + 9 days in July (30 − 21 = 9) = **July 9, 2028**. **(d) Alternative facts (no December trip; files I-765 on February 22, 2027; travels May 20–June 5, 2027 while I-765 is pending):** **No, she does NOT need Form I-539.** Because she had not departed the U.S. before filing Form I-765 on February 22, 2027 (on or before March 18, 2027), she qualified for the **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i)** Form I-539 exemption when filing; and when she later departs while Form I-765 is pending, **8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(ii)** preserves her pending I-765, the second sentence of **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(ii)** directs that she be admitted pursuant to **8 CFR 214.1(a)**, and **8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(D)** recognizes CBP admission after travel as satisfying fixed-stay authorization without an I-539. **Readmission period:** Under **8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(iii)**, with a pending Form I-765, CBP may admit her until the **DSO's recommended OPT end date on Form I-20 (June 9, 2028) plus the 30-day period in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v)** = **July 9, 2028** (note travel converts her from the 60-day transition rule to a 30-day departure period). **What she should carry:** Per **8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(iii)** and **8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(iii)** (and 91 FR 45098, 45100), she should carry: (1) her **USCIS Form I-797C receipt notice** for the pending Form I-765; (2) her **DSO-endorsed Form I-20** recommending post-completion OPT through June 9, 2028 (with valid travel signature); and (3) a **valid passport and valid F-1 visa** (plus arrangements to monitor any USCIS RFE or EAD delivery at her U.S. address, 91 FR 45100 fn. 303).
Q13.basis: **Final regulatory text (FR Doc. 2026-14439):** 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A) and (iii) (91 FR 45122); 8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(ii)–(iii) (91 FR 45123); 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i)–(ii) (91 FR 45123, Form I-539 exemption on or before Mar. 18, 2027, loss of exemption if departing before filing I-765, and admission under 214.1(a) if departing while I-765 is pending); 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i) and (v) (91 FR 45124–45125); 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B) and (vi) (91 FR 45126); 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(D) (91 FR 45127); and 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i)(B)(2) and (D) (91 FR 45124). **Preamble explanation:** Section IV.F.1 (91 FR 45017), Section V.B (91 FR 45098), Section V.D (91 FR 45100 & fn. 303), and Section V.E.1 (91 FR 45101).
Q13.uncertainty: In part (b), 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(ii) states the student must file both Form I-765 and Form I-539 'pursuant to Sec. 214.2(f)(11)(i)(B)(2)'; while 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B) makes an I-539 timely if received by June 13, 2027, 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i)(B)(2) also requires filing within 30 days after the DSO enters the OPT recommendation in SEVIS, so filing Form I-539 concurrently with Form I-765 on February 22, 2027 avoids any risk that USCIS applies the 30-day DSO-recommendation window to both forms. In part (d), preamble fn. 303 (91 FR 45100) notes ICE guidance warning that if USCIS *approves* the OPT Form I-765 while Sofia is abroad (May 20–June 5, 2027), CBP may expect her to have the physical EAD card in hand upon re-entry.

Q14.answer: **(a) Document behind the '$70,000 / $30,000 OPT' report:** *Optional Practical Training Fees*, FR Doc. **2026-20660**, **91 FR 64566–64600** (published **October 8, 2026**); Type: **Proposed Rule** (Notice of Proposed Rulemaking / NPRM); Agency: **U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), Department of Homeland Security (DHS)**; Docket: **DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100**; RIN: **1653-AB01**. **Current status and deadlines:** It is a **proposed rule only—not finalized and not in force** as of November 14, 2026. It sets three deadlines/timeframes: (1) **November 9, 2026** for public comments on the NPRM (closed five days ago); (2) **December 7, 2026** for Paperwork Reduction Act comments on the information collection (still open, 91 FR 64566); and (3) a proposed effective date / fee start date of **60 days after publication of the final rule** in the Federal Register (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(3), 91 FR 64577, 64600). **(b) Amount that would apply to Daniel's April 2027 STEM OPT extension if finalized as proposed:** **$70,000 (NOT $30,000).** Under proposed **8 CFR 214.13(i)(2)** (91 FR 64600), the $30,000 subsequent OPT fee applies only *'if the alien has previously participated in OPT **and paid the initial OPT fee of $70,000**,'* and proposed **8 CFR 214.13(i)(3)** (*Transition period*, 91 FR 64600) explicitly requires schools recommending *'any type of OPT'* on or after the effective date to pay **$70,000**, with the $30,000 fee applying *'[t]hereafter'* only to students *'for which the $70,000 OPT fee has been paid'* (confirmed in the preamble/RIA at 91 FR 64577, 64583, 64594: during the transition, STEM OPT recommendations for students who never had the $70,000 fee paid require **$70,000**). Because Daniel's 2026–2027 post-completion OPT predated the fee, no $70,000 fee was ever paid for him. **(c) Who pays, when, consequences of nonpayment, and refundability:** Under proposed **8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i)–(iii)** and **8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2)** (91 FR 64577, 64599–64600): **Who pays:** The **SEVP-certified educational institution (school)**. **When:** **Before the DSO issues/enters the OPT recommendation in SEVIS** (the school pays first, the DSO confirms payment in SEVIS and issues a signed, dated Form I-20 confirming fee payment, and only then may the student file Form I-765). **If not paid:** The **DSO is prohibited from entering the OPT recommendation in SEVIS**, and **USCIS may not grant OPT employment authorization** if the DSO recommended OPT before payment or if the school failed to pay all applicable OPT fees. **Refundability:** **Once the OPT/STEM OPT EAD is issued/granted, the fee is strictly non-refundable under any circumstances.** *Before* the EAD/extension is issued, the school (after the DSO removes the OPT recommendation in SEVIS) may request a refund, which **SEVP adjudicates in its discretion on a case-by-case basis** with **no administrative appeal**. **(d) From when the fee applies, and whether earlier DSO recommendation timing could keep Daniel outside it:** Under proposed **8 CFR 214.13(i)(3)**, the fee applies to **DSO recommendations dated on or after the final rule's effective date** (proposed as 60 days after final rule publication). **Yes, earlier DSO recommendation timing could keep Daniel outside the fee, depending on when any final rule takes effect:** under existing **8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i)(C)**, Daniel can file his STEM OPT Form I-765 up to **90 days before** his June 30, 2027 EAD expires—i.e., as early as **April 1, 2027** (29 remaining days in Apr [30 − 1] + 31 in May + 30 in Jun = 90 days)—and the DSO's SEVIS STEM OPT recommendation is valid for **60 days** prior to filing Form I-765, meaning the DSO could issue and date the STEM OPT recommendation as early as **January 31, 2027** (for an April 1 I-765 filing: 28 days in Feb 2027 + 31 in Mar + 1 in Apr = 60 days) or **February 11, 2027** (for his planned April 12 I-765 filing: 17 remaining days in Feb [28 − 11] + 31 in Mar + 12 in Apr = 60 days). Because PRA comments run through December 7, 2026 (so a final rule with a 60-day effective date could not take effect before early February 2027 at the absolute earliest, and likely later), **a valid DSO recommendation dated before the final rule's effective date would exempt Daniel entirely**. **(e) Under the rules IN FORCE TODAY (November 14, 2026):** Because Daniel will file on **April 12, 2027**—which is **after March 18, 2027** (and even his earliest eligible 90-day filing date of April 1, 2027 is after March 18, 2027)—he does **not** qualify for the pre-March 18, 2027 Form I-539 exemption in 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i) (unless DHS extends it by FR notice under 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(iii)). Therefore: (1) **What he must file:** **Both Form I-765** (for the 24-month STEM OPT extension, with fee, Form I-20 endorsed within 60 days, and Form I-983 training plan requirements under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(C) and (f)(11)(i)(C)) **AND Form I-539** (EOS application with fee, biometrics if required, financial evidence, and endorsed Form I-20 under **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)**, **8 CFR 214.1(c)(2)**, and **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(v)**), received by USCIS before June 30, 2027; (2) **Work authorization while pending:** Under **8 CFR 274a.12(b)(6)(iv)** (confirmed at 91 FR 45101, and unaffected by FR Doc. 2026-20955), his OPT work authorization is **automatically extended for up to 180 days** after June 30, 2027 while the timely STEM OPT I-765 is pending—through **December 27, 2027** (31 in Jul + 31 in Aug + 30 in Sep + 31 in Oct + 30 in Nov = 153 + 27 in Dec = 180 days)—and his stay remains authorized under **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii)**; (3) **Authorized stay if approved:** His 24-month STEM OPT EAD runs July 1, 2027 through **June 30, 2029**, plus a **30-day** departure period under **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(vi)** and **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v)** (91 FR 45105, 45125–45126) = **July 30, 2029**.
Q14.basis: **Proposed rule (not yet final):** FR Doc. 2026-20660, *Optional Practical Training Fees*, 91 FR 64566–64600 (Oct. 8, 2026; DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100; RIN 1653-AB01), specifically `DATES` (91 FR 64566), Section V.A–C (91 FR 64576–64577), Section VII.A–B (91 FR 64583, 64594), and proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i)–(iii) and 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(3) (91 FR 64599–64600). **Final regulatory text in force (FR Doc. 2026-14439):** 8 CFR 214.1(c)(2), (m)(1), and (m)(1)(i), (iii) (91 FR 45122–45123); 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v), (viii) and (f)(7)(iii), (v), (vi) (91 FR 45125–45126); preamble at 91 FR 45101, 45105 (confirming 8 CFR 274a.12(b)(6)(iv) 180-day STEM OPT auto-extension and 30-day departure period on EOS approvals); plus existing 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i)(C) and 8 CFR 274a.12(b)(6)(iv).
Q14.uncertainty: In part (b), there is a slight drafting awkwardness between proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1) (which describes the $70,000 fee as applying 'the first time that the alien is recommended to participate in OPT') and proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(2)–(3) (which require $70,000 for any OPT recommendation on or after the effective date unless the $70,000 fee was previously paid), though proposed (i)(3) and the preamble/RIA (91 FR 64577, 64583, 64594) unambiguously resolve this at $70,000. Also, DHS solicited comment on an alternative applying $70,000 again after each degree-level change (91 FR 64577). In part (e), if DHS publishes a Federal Register notice under 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(iii) extending the March 18, 2027 Form I-539 exemption by 6 months, Daniel would not need Form I-539 and would receive a 60-day departure period through August 29, 2029 under 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i).

Q15.answer: **1. Incorrect.** Under **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B)** and **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v)** (final regulatory text, 91 FR 45125–45126), an EOS application is timely if USCIS receives it **on or before the date the authorized period of stay expires, which *includes* the 30-day departure period** on Form I-94 (or the 60-day departure period for D/S transition students under 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1), 91 FR 45101)—and conversely, for a >4-year program, the 4-year I-94 expires *years before* the I-20 program end date. Only the *DSO's SEVIS program extension* must precede the current I-20 end date (**8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(viii)**), and filing before the departure period is needed only to preserve automatic employment extension (**8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii)**). *Reworded:* 'USCIS must receive an extension-of-stay application on or before the student's authorized stay expires (including the 30-day departure period on Form I-94, or 60 days for D/S transition students), though any DSO extension of a current I-20 end date must be entered in SEVIS on or before that I-20 end date, and USCIS must receive the application before the departure period begins for the student to keep working while it is pending.' **2. Incorrect** (for arrivals during the 30-day pre-program window). **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)** (91 FR 45124) states that the up-to-30-day pre-start arrival period and 30-day post-end departure period *'do not count toward the maximum length of stay,'* and the preamble (**91 FR 45098**) explicitly confirms the 4-year maximum is counted **from the Form I-20 program start (or report) date, not the date of entry**. *Reworded:* 'For a student entering during the 30-day arrival window before a program begins, the four-year maximum admission period is counted from the Form I-20 program start or report date—not the date of entry—and neither the 30-day arrival period nor the 30-day departure period counts toward the four years.' **3. Correct** (assuming the student filed *before* the 30-day departure period so on-campus work was auto-extended during those 240 days). Under **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii)** (91 FR 45125–45126; preamble **91 FR 45043, 45106**), timely EOS filing extends authorized stay and full-time study *until USCIS issues a decision*, whereas on-campus employment is auto-extended for **no more than 240 days** from the Form I-94 expiration date (and not at all if filed during the 30-day departure period). *Refined wording:* 'If USCIS has still not decided an extension application timely filed before the departure period 240 days after the I-94 expiration date, the student remains in authorized stay and may keep studying full-time until USCIS decides the case, but must stop any on-campus job after day 240 (or before the departure period if filed during the 30-day departure window).' **4. Incorrect.** **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)(A)** (91 FR 45124) restricts standalone English language training (ELT) students to a **maximum 24-month admission period** (plus 30 days). Although **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(i)(C)(2)(ii)** and **(f)(7)(vi)** (91 FR 45126) allow medical EOS requests generally 'not to exceed 4 years' without repeating the ELT cap, **(f)(5)(i)(A)** sets the overarching stay limit and the preamble (**91 FR 45039**; see also **91 FR 44979, 45103, 45110**) explicitly resolves this: **'Students who encounter extenuating circumstances such as illness, disability, or other emergencies during their studies, will still be limited to the 24-month admission period'** (except integrated degree-pathway students at the same institution or pre-Sept. 15, 2026 D/S transition students finishing a current I-20, 91 FR 45039). *Reworded:* 'A student in a standalone English language training program is subject to an aggregate lifetime limit of 24 months (plus 30 days) and may extend on medical grounds only up to—never beyond—that 24-month cap.' **5. Incorrect.** Under **8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A)**, **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)**, and **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(i)(C)(1)** (91 FR 45122, 45124, 45126), the 4-year cap limits the *I-94 admission period*, not the academic program or Form I-20; DHS's preamble (**91 FR 45039**) flatly states *'That is untrue. If the program has been accredited as a 5-year program, the I-20 ... will state the full program length,'* and the student uses that same I-20 to apply for an EOS before the 4-year stay expires. *Reworded:* 'An accredited five-year degree program is still issued on a single Form I-20 showing the full five-year program length; CBP admits the student for four years (plus arrival/departure periods), and the student applies for an extension of stay (or travels and re-enters) before that stay expires to finish the fifth year.' **6. Partly correct (with a regulatory-text vs. preamble conflict where the regulatory text controls).** While **8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A)–(B)**, **8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(ii)**, **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(ii)**, and **8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(D)** (91 FR 45122–45123, 45127) allow CBP, *in its discretion* ('may be admitted'), to grant up to 4 years (+ 30 days) when a student re-enters after prior stay expired, with a pending EOS, from D/S, or for OPT, **Preamble Section V.B (91 FR 45098)** broadly says *any* student departing without an approved EOS may be readmitted up to the Form I-20 end date (not to exceed 4 years), whereas **controlling final regulatory text in 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A)–(C) (91 FR 45122)** omits continuing fixed-date students whose current stay has *not* expired and who have *no* EOS pending or approved (leaving them reliant on general 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)); moreover, CBP admission is discretionary, capped at 4 years, unavailable for extending stay under contiguous-territory automatic visa revalidation (**8 CFR 214.1(b)(1)** limits admission to the *unexpired* prior stay), and requires any SEVIS extension to precede the old I-20 end date (**8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(viii)**). *Reworded:* 'A student with a valid F-1 visa who travels abroad and is readmitted with a timely updated Form I-20 may, in CBP's discretion, receive a new I-94 up to the I-20 end date (not to exceed four years, plus 30 days) and does not need a USCIS extension for whatever period CBP actually grants on the new I-94—except that automatic visa revalidation only restores the previously unexpired stay, and students traveling mid-stay without a pending EOS must check their new I-94 because of a drafting gap in 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i).' **7. Incorrect (and the regulatory text controls over conflicting preamble passages).** Although one preamble summary refers loosely to *'the first 6 months after the rule takes effect'* (**91 FR 44978**) and another preamble sentence contains a typo saying *'on or before September 15, 2026'* (**91 FR 45101**), **the binding final regulatory text at 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i) (91 FR 45123; matched at 91 FR 45017, 45031, 45033–45034) controls and sets the deadline as *'on or before March 18, 2027'*** (extendable by FR notice under 214.1(m)(1)(iii)); furthermore, the exemption applies **only** to D/S transition students who have **not** traveled and re-entered on a fixed-date I-94 before filing (**8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(ii)**) and only for post-completion OPT or STEM OPT. *Reworded:* 'For D/S transition F-1 students who were maintaining status on September 15, 2026 and have not traveled and re-entered on a fixed-date I-94 before filing, the Form I-539 exemption for post-completion OPT or STEM OPT covers timely Form I-765 applications filed on or before March 18, 2027.'
Q15.uncertainty: In Statement 3, as noted in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii) (91 FR 45125–45126), sentence 2 counts the 240-day employment auto-extension from the Form I-94 expiration date while sentence 5 (for Form I-9 verification) counts 240 days from the employment end date 30 days before the I-94 date. In Statement 4, while 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(vi) omits a cross-reference to 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)(A)'s 24-month ELT cap, reading (f)(5)(i)(A) and the preamble (91 FR 45039, 45110) together establishes that ELT stays cannot exceed 24 months.

Q16.answer: **(a) Admit-until date on Lin's initial Form I-94:** **September 22, 2031.** Because Lin's six-year PhD program (August 23, 2027 to May 14, 2033) exceeds 4 years, under **8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A)**, **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)**, and **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v)** (final regulatory text) she is admitted for the **4-year maximum period of admission**, **plus a 30-day departure period**. Crucially, under **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)** (and preamble **91 FR 45098**), her pre-start arrival window (from her August 2, 2027 entry to her August 23, 2027 program start date) **does not count** toward the 4-year maximum; the 4 years run from the **August 23, 2027** program start date. *Date arithmetic:* August 23, 2027 + 4 years = **August 23, 2031**; adding the 30-day departure period: 8 remaining days in August (31 − 23 = 8, reaching August 31, 2031) + 22 days in September (30 − 8 = 22) = **September 22, 2031**. **(b) Staying beyond that date—procedure, submissions, ground, earliest filing, and new end date:** Without qualifying travel/readmission, Lin must **timely file Form I-539** (*Application to Extend/Change Nonimmigrant Status*, or successor form) with USCIS on or before **September 22, 2031** (**8 CFR 214.1(c)(2)**, **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B)**—and on or before **August 23, 2031** to auto-extend any on-campus assistantship under **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii)**). Q16.uncertainty: In part (a), DHS's anniversary arithmetic in 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1) (counting 4 years from Sept. 15, 2026 to Sept. 15, 2030 + 30 days = Oct. 15, 2030) yields August 23, 2031 + 30 days = September 22, 2031; if CBP systems instead compute a 4-year period on an inclusive day-before-anniversary basis (Aug. 22, 2031 + 30 days), the I-94 could read September 21, 2031. In part (d), as explained above, the regulatory text of 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A)–(C) leaves open how CBP will treat a mid-stay readmission where the prior fixed I-94 has not expired and no EOS is pending or approved, making inspection of the actual post-travel Form I-94 essential.
